utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, you can have the accused brought into the courtroom, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Everyone is ready, the counsel for the Prosecution, the counsel for the Defence, the accused also, I believe. Without further delay, Mr. Hayman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and good morning. Good morning, Your Honours. This is a day we've all been looking forward to greatly, not because the Defence is arguing but, of course, because it is the last day of the trial. I concluded yesterday at 5.30 in the morning on the 16th of April. Blaskic had issued the three orders, the written orders, we've discussed, and at roughly 5.30, we know the BH army shells the Hotel Vitez and the military police attack Ahmici. Exactly what the timing there is, we don't know. The evidence isn't clear. But both of those events appear to have occurred around the same time. It is not illogical, Your Honours, that when fighting broke out, chaos broke out, because all of these locations around Vitez are within earshot. You can hear detonations. We ask you to think about the minds of particularly the militia men, the men conscripted into the Vitez Brigade in the prior few weeks, and think about their reaction when they heard gunfire, they heard shells, they'd seen the TV reports of Totic's kidnapping and the murders, they'd seen the bodies, and then the firing starts. There was a lot of fear and there was certainly some panic on the part of both BH army soldiers and HVO militia. What happened in Ahmici with respect to the military police was different. But in and around Vitez, those appear to be the themes that bind events in and around Stari Vitez and Vitez. What happened in the hotel? You heard in excruciating detail from General Blaskic about what happened on the 16th, 17th, and 18th and so forth of April, as recorded in the operative diary of the Operative Zone which General Blaskic had a chance to review in late 1995 before he voluntarily came here to The Hague, and he took notes from that operative diary, and he provided you with all that detail. Indeed, I think he testified for three months, the better part of three months. He gave a great amount of detail, Your Honours, and the Prosecution had every opportunity to come in in their rebuttal case and impeach and contradict General Blaskic's testimony with evidence. They chose not to do that. They chose instead to launch verbal assaults on his honour and his credibility in their argument. I will address every one of those assaults when I'm done with the chronology of events. But we ask you to keep in mind that he gave a great amount of detail so that his account could be checked, could be confirmed, or proven otherwise. You will have to decide. Have they proven his detailed minute-by-minute account to be inaccurate in any material respects? In the basement of the hotel, there were two regular telephones, as he described, and of course he could get packet communications from the PTT building. They had to be sent and opened and walked across, or whatever was going on in terms of courier deliveries at the time, but those were his lines of communication. And as he described, beginning at the first moment, the Hotel Vitez began to receive panicked calls from all kinds of people, civilians, political figures, other military units, and so forth. You have the reports he received. You have his verbal description of the oral reports he received. You have the written reports he received. They're in evidence. There is no evidence, based on all those reports, that he failed to act during the period 16 April to 20 April, based on any information he received of crimes that were ongoing or crimes that were likely to be committed. And that is why the Prosecution asserts in their argument that Blaskic wasn't in the Hotel Vitez on the 16th of April. They assert now in argument that he was out in the field, not in the hotel, not in the basement operations room, and they do that because they have to get him out of the hotel because it's apparent that if you're in the basement of the hotel, you're entirely dependent on information that's coming in. You have no ability to make your own observations. What is the basis of that assertion? They say that Stewart went to the hotel at 10.00 in the morning and was told Blaskic was not there. That is what the Prosecutor told you. But if you look in the reporter's transcript at 28830, lines 2 to 19, Stewart says he spoke to a sentry, a guard, and was told that there no one was available to see him. He was not told that Blaskic was not in the headquarters, as Mr. Kehoe told you. He was told that there was no one available to see him. He was not told whether Blaskic was there or not. The Prosecutor also asserts that an EC Monitor was also told on the 16th of April, when his colleague, another EC Monitor called the hotel, that "Blaskic was not in his headquarters." That's a quote from the Prosecutor's argument. Is that true? The quote they provided is that of Lars Baggesen. Baggesen did not make the call. Remi Landry made the call. They were together. Remi Landry testified in this case, and I asked him exactly what he was told when he called the hotel, and here's what he said. (Videotape played) "A We tried to communicate with the HVO headquarters in order to speak with the people in positions of authority, and according to my notes -- my notes indicate that I tried to communicate with the HVO commander, Colonel Blaskic, but I was told that he was not available."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So both of the witness accounts are that they called -- either they spoke to a sentry or they called the main number on the morning of the 16th. They were not told that Blaskic wasn't there. They were told that he wasn't available to speak with you now. What do you expect in the middle of combat? We don't know if the message was even relayed to then Colonel Blaskic. We do know that he wanted to communicate and make contact with UNPROFOR because he sent two negotiators to the Bila base at noon on the 16th to try and negotiate a cease-fire. That's in the record in this case. Marko Prskalo and Zoran Pilicic, they went on the 16th, they went again on the 17th and were shot by snipers from Stari Vitez as they were re-entering the Hotel Vitez. The Prosecution asks you to speculate and disregard the evidence concerning where then Colonel Blaskic was on the morning of the 16th of April. Is there any evidence that he was in the field? After two years of scrutinising witness testimony, documents, is there any evidence he was in the field on the 16th, 17th, 18th, or 19th of April? Not even Cicko says he was in the field, the one person we know who's out to get Colonel Blaskic. No one says he was in the field. There is no evidence he was in the field. As professional Judges, you know what it means when the facts are scrutinised, facts regarding any event, are scrutinised with as much detail as they have been in this case involving years of trial and decades of attorney time and investigative time. There isn't any evidence that he was out in the field during those days. You know what that means. It means he wasn't out in the field. He was in the basement of the Hotel Vitez, which is the responsible place for him to be at the time, given his responsibilities and the danger, which I will speak about, that existed in the region during that period. On the 16th, he was told that the HVO had lost their positions on Kuber. He was told that the position of the HVO in Zenica was desperate and chaotic. Those were the reports he was getting. Your Honours know from Defence Exhibit 194 that the BH army was, in fact, advancing from Zenica towards Vitez on the 16th. That's a BH army order at the brigade level which recounts an order from Hadzihasanovic on the morning of the 16th, sometime prior to noon, to move, to move towards Vitez. Defence Exhibit 194, BH army order to advance on Vitez on the 16th of April. Was it in reaction to the attack in Ahmici on the morning? Perhaps. We're not suggesting we know exactly what the chronology there was. But the point is, on the 16th, Blaskic is receiving information that the BH army, with their 30.000 troops in Zenica, are moving towards Vitez, and they were, and you know that because, among other things, of Defence Exhibit 194. What did he hear from the military police in Ahmici? He heard from them at 11.42 a.m. He's able to give you that level of detail because of his notes. As you recall, the main staff had told then Colonel Blaskic that the military police and the Vitezovi would be attached to him in the case of an all-out BH army attack. Such attachment occurs when the subordinate commander first notifies the superior commander. In that phone call, Pasko Ljubicic told Blaskic that the fighting with the BH army was fierce in Ahmici and centred around the school, the mosque, and individual homes. There was no mention of any attack by the military police on Ahmici, no mention of any civilian casualties, and no mention that the village had been razed. The Defence position is that this report was intentionally false, it was incomplete, and it was wholly misleading. Why is that? Because Colonel Blaskic would not have condoned in any way the intentional killing of civilians, the burning of civilian structures without military necessity, and Pasko Ljubicic knew that. He also knew he had disobeyed Blaskic's order, Defence Exhibit 267. So he had strong motives to give a false report to Blaskic. You are fully aware of the falsities in the report. The Prosecutor's case did show that by mid morning on the 17th, within two or three hours of the attack on Ahmici, the military police had already moved through much of the village, executing civilians, killing prisoners, and setting fire to houses. There was some continued fighting going on but most of the killing, if not all, appeared to have occurred in those first few hours. Now, they attack Blaskic's testimony for saying that, but what he said is that what he heard in this courtroom. You heard the same evidence. You judge. Is that what the Prosecutor demonstrated? In the afternoon of the 16th, Blaskic issued a written order to Ljubicic demanding more information about what the military police activities were in Ahmici. Yesterday, you saw the responsive report, D280, which has a reference line and references Blaskic's request. Again, does that fit in with the Prosecutor's theory? He did receive a written report later, that is D280, it was also false. Was the falsity of that report apparent on its face? Should the seven members of the headquarters staff, including Colonel Blaskic, who got that report on the late afternoon or evening of the 16th, D280, should they have said, "This obviously is untrue" and taken other measures? Now, Colonel Stewart said that he thought that they should have or perhaps they should have perceived that it was false because he thought that it was unlikely that the school and the mosque would be areas of fighting because the mosque is a poor defensive position. Colonel Stewart, we respect his opinion, he's entitled to his opinion, but he didn't have any specific information about the fact that there were BH army units in Ahmici. He didn't know that they had plans to form defensive lines, where those lines were, and what weapons they had and so forth, and you know now from the diary, D197, that all those things existed and that hence Exhibit D280 was not prima facie, unrealistic or incredible in any way. For now, I'd like to follow the trail, as Colonel Blaskic followed it, of that false report, D280. Given the resources that Colonel Blaskic had at the time, he stayed in the hotel during the period 16 to 19 of April. The Prosecutor doesn't claim, at least not after the morning of the 16th, that he was anywhere else, and they haven't presented any evidence that he was anywhere else, nor do they claim that he avoided knowledge or failed to make reasonable efforts to acquire information during that time period. The fact is if you look at his chronology, and perhaps you want some of your staff to outline it for you, you will see that he was active during the period trying to acquire better and more information so as to keep himself informed of what was going on in the many different locations where there was combat and conflict. That is the duty and responsibility of a commander. On the afternoon of the 16th, he was told by those two negotiators, HVO negotiators, who were returning to the hotel, that they saw a body, not in uniform, who appeared to be civilian in the street in Vitez while driving back through the window of a Warrior. This was not in Ahmici. It was in Vitez itself. Did Blaskic respond to that information or did he not care because CNN had not broadcast about it? He responded as he worked in the early morning hours of 17th April. He was concerned about the fall of Kuber, he was concerned about the deteriorating HVO positions, but at 4.00 in the morning on the 17th of April, in Defence Exhibit 284, he still took time to tell his units the following: "Soldiers are to be specifically cautioned about how to treat civilians, the elderly, women and children who are not to be killed, because that is a CRIME," with "crime" in all caps. He wrote that at 4.00 in the morning on the 17th of April and sent it to all units. He also sought a cease-fire on the 16th. He ordered a cease-fire at 16.00 on the 16th, that is Defence 279. It did not hold. He sent his two negotiators back to the Hotel Vitez on the 17th to try and implement the cease-fire, and they were shot while trying to reenter the Hotel Vitez, which reduced the number of staff in the hotel from seven to five. When you're considering whether it was reasonable and prudent for Colonel Blaskic to stay in the basement of the hotel during that dangerous time, please keep in mind that two of his seven staff members were shot on the 17th on the steps of the Hotel Vitez. On the 18th, there was a cease-fire agreement between Izetbegovic and Boban, and they ordered, as part of that cease-fire, that information should be gathered as to the protagonists of the conflict and the killing of captured soldiers and civilians. That's Defence 316. Those orders went to all units in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and contained no specific information about any crimes or misconduct in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Blaskic repeated that order, as he was duty-bound to do. The cease-fire still did not hold, and the HVO position continued to deteriorate. On the 20th of April, the first high level cease-fire meeting occurred in the Lasva Valley, and it was in Zenica. To help Your Honours track the process of the discovery and investigation of Ahmici, we have made a timeline, and I'd like to hand out copies of that timeline, please. I won't be referring to all of the images on this timeline, but we will be referring to some. There are also some entries, Mr. President, that refer to either closed-session testimony or under-seal documents, so I won't put all of the slides up on the monitor. I think I can do this in open session by simply not referring to certain entries and not putting certain slides up on the monitors. There may be a few parts which I will need to refer to in private session. First, on the top of the package, you have a timeline spanning the entire period from April until October of 1994, and I'll come back to that. It provides a bit of an overview. The second slide which I also have on your monitors now, is April 1993. If you track from left to right, you see on the 20th of April, Colonel Blaskic leaves the Hotel Vitez to go to the meeting in Zenica. What happens in Zenica? There's a meeting. The cease-fire is the topic. But in the course of the meeting, outside of the formal discussions, Dzemo Merdan makes the comment that there are 500 dead civilians in a canal down by the road near Vitez. That is the comment according to the evidence. Merdan did not mention Ahmici. Every witness to testify about that meeting has told you that Ahmici was not mentioned in any form in the 20th of April meeting. You can refer to Witness ZZ at reporter's transcript 10924, and you can refer to a protected court witness at reporter's transcript 93983 (sic). Blaskic responded to Merdan that if that was true, there should be a joint investigation immediately, but there was no discussion at the meeting either of Merdan's claim or of Blaskic's proposal. It appears that Merdan's comment, if it was even made to international observers present, it appeared to them it was a negotiating tactic, not a serious accusation. Still, Blaskic did not ignore it. He was concerned about it, and when he come back to the hotel late that night, he asked his staff to check for any reports that might tend to even substantiate Merdan's claim. He was told there were none. That's in his testimony at transcript 18880. Now, if he ordered an attack on Ahmici, why would he ask his staff to check the documents to see if there were reports of civilian casualties in the area of Vitez? The next day, the 21st of April, there was another meeting to implement the cease-fire held at the ECMM house in Nova Bila. That's not on our timeline because, again, the witnesses indicate there was no mention whatsoever made at that meeting, including by the BH army, of any civilian casualties in the region. No mention whatsoever of Ahmici. You can see Mr. Watters testimony at transcript page 3496, as well as a protected court witness at transcript page 23615. What happened then? We all know very well what happened. On the 22nd of April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, could you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. Colonel Stewart, while policing the buffer zone that was trying to be established found BH army troops who refused to pull back from the buffer zone, and with good reason, Your Honours. They were enraged and outraged because they had heard of murdered civilians in Ahmici. Gasoline had been poured on the fire of conflict, tension, and hatred in the Lasva Valley. That was the effect of the Ahmici massacre. Gasoline was poured on the fire. Stewart went to Ahmici, and after a careful inspection, he found eight bodies, two outside of a structure and six more in a cellar of a burned and collapsed house. It was a tragedy, what he found, but again, even after this careful inspection, he found eight bodies. He didn't find 100 or 50 or 75. He didn't find visible evidence of an immense massacre, he found eight bodies. He sent a letter on that same day to Colonel Blaskic, which you know, telling him again that he has found eight bodies, again a terrible tragedy, even those eight, but it's significant what he found, and asking for help in investigating this crime. Has the Prosecution proven that Blaskic received this information before the 22nd of April? You need to decide that to judge this case. From the makeshift command post in the basement of the Hotel Vitez, could he make visual or oral observations, indicating that there was a crime in Ahmici ongoing on the 16th of April? The basement of the Hotel Vitez, Your Honours, is still there to this day. It is available for scientific or forensic analysis and inspection, sound tests, visual tests. That evidence could have been presented to you. The Prosecutor made no effort, no attempt, or perhaps -- well, we assume, in good faith, they simply made no attempt to determine what could be heard or seen from that basement. Instead, they offered general opinions that, from a distance of five kilometres, yes, you can see smoke, and smoke means there's a crime ongoing. When witnesses were asked the relevant question, namely, what could you detect from the basement about the nature of combat or other violence in the Vitez area? The answer was uniform from each one of them, and this is a very telling passage that I'm going to play for you now, Your Honours. Sefkija Dzidic. (Videotape played) "Mr. Kehoe: Q So if you were in the Hotel Vitez, you could see virtually all of the activity taking place on the attacks of these villages and hear the gunfire and the shelling on those villages; is that correct? A The shooting would be heard. From a hotel room, it could be seen, but it could neither be heard nor seen if a person would -- if a person had been in the cellar, but only in that case could they fail to see and hear."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked Mr. Dzidic about the Hotel Vitez, from the Hotel Vitez. He didn't mention the cellar. Why did Sefkija Dzidic volunteer his comment about the cellar, that you couldn't hear or see anything from the cellar? It wasn't in the question. The Court can review the entire transcript at page 1268. For Judge Rodrigues's benefit, Sefkija Dzidic was the Territorial Defence commander in Stari Vitez. He spent the whole war in Stari Vitez. Why did he immediately go to the cellar in his answer? Because he lived through the war in Vitez. He knows that when there's shelling and sniper fire, you go in the cellar. You want to live? You go in the cellar. And that's why he volunteered, even though it was unresponsive to the answer, that you couldn't hear anything or see anything from the cellar of the Hotel Vitez. Dzidic knew where he'd be if he was in the Hotel Vitez during that conflict. He would have gone to the cellar, clearly. Now, the Prosecutor relies on a visit to Ahmici by Mr. Jozic on the 21st of April, and statements by Cerkez and Valenta on or about the 19th that involve vague references to Ahmici, did you hear about Ahmici, and that sort of thing. None of these facts established that any of these persons knew there had been a massacre on the 19th or 20th of April, and they certainly do not establish that Blaskic knew that was the case. We know, Your Honours, that the Dutch Battalion was located at Santici across the road from Ahmici. The Dutch Battalion, you haven't heard very much about them. They were not co-located with BritBat. They were not in Vitez. They were not in Busovaca. They were in Santici, across the road from Ahmici. You can look at the maps in this case, and you can see exactly where that base was. And the British Battalion, of course, had dozens and dozens of patrols out from the 16th of April onwards. Did any of those patrols or did the DutchBat troops, that had a permanent location across the road from Ahmici, did they hear the sounds or see the images of a massacre on the morning of the 16th of April from their vantage points, or were those sounds and images indistinguishable from those of combat operations, operations which, in fact, were ongoing at the time in more than a dozen locations around, as well as inside, Vitez itself? The question was answered by the BritBat witnesses. They didn't see a massacre. And with respect to DutchBat, the question is answered by the Prosecution's failure to call a single DutchBat witness to testify on that subject. In your packets, Your Honour, there is another table which I think is the last page, if this isn't clear on the screen -- oh, I'm sorry. We need to go into private session to look at this chart. My apologies. Yes, I think we need private session, I think that would be best, just for a moment, and we need the video monitor in the public gallery turned off. utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We return then to Colonel Stewart's letter. What did Blaskic do? He responded the next day to Colonel Stewart's letter, and he also ordered his staff to collect all documents within the Operative Zone, orders and reports, from the 16th to the 22nd of April, so that they would be available for an investigation, and his letter you have. You are familiar with it. He asked for Stewart and for Stewart to enlist Thebault's help in convening the chiefs of staff of the BH army and the HVO to address the situation and build support for a joint investigation of the crime in Ahmici. The fact is a joint investigation into Ahmici was a very good idea, both on Colonel Stewart's part and with respect to Colonel Blaskic's support for it. Only UNPROFOR and the ECMM could pressure the chiefs of the main staff to give support to an investigation. Only UNPROFOR had secure transport to move the joint commission members around safely, and only the U.N. or the BH army could effectively interview the survivors, the surviving victims who were either in Zenica or were certainly in no emotional condition to be interrogated by HVO military policemen or SIS representatives. Was Colonel Blaskic's request for an investigation sincere? The Prosecution has to argue that it wasn't because otherwise their theory falls apart. What other evidence is there of his state of mind at the time? On the 24th of April, he met with Colonel Stewart, and Stewart personally briefed him on what he had seen on the 22nd and, I believe, on the 23rd when he returned with Martin Bell to Ahmici. Stewart described Blaskic's reaction at that meeting to the news, to his description, and he said, "Blaskic was absolutely horrified" at what had taken place in Ahmici, absolutely horrified. That was quoted in the press, Defence Exhibit 592, and confirmed by Colonel Stewart's testimony at transcript page 23815. While Colonel Blaskic still hoped for a joint investigation, he didn't wait for that support, and on the 24th of April, he gave a verbal order to SIS to investigate Ahmici. Why SIS? Why not the military police? They were the body that had a whole department dedicated to criminal investigation? The military police could not be entrusted with investigating themselves. That's a basic principle, if one wishes to seek integrity for an investigation. You do not entrust a suspect to investigate him or herself. Those of us that have had prosecutive or other criminal, judicial experience or inspector general experience in any agency of any national government, we know that that is a fundamental principle. There were no entities, other than the military police and the SIS, that had any investigative skills or experience. What if Blaskic had ordered the Vitez Brigade to investigate Ahmici. Militia men, villagers, could they do that job, or would he be on trial now for incompetence in trying to follow-up and cause an investigation? Only SIS, other than the military police, had any expertise in criminal investigations, and only SIS had the authority to investigate the military police because SIS had authority for security matters over all entities within the structure of the Ministry of Defence. Blaskic had no option other than to ask SIS to investigate. There was no one else. The Prosecutor has not suggested that he had any other option. Within three days of ordering SIS to investigate, Blaskic himself toured Ahmici on the 27th of April, and after his inspection, he attended a press conference in Busovaca and made a clear statement denouncing the crime and calling for public support for an investigation. His exact words were recorded in contemporaneous notes by Martin Bell, and you heard from the honourable Mr. Bell in this courtroom. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Did then Colonel Blaskic address the subject of the massacre in Ahmici at this press conference? A Yes, he did. I made some notes at the time which I, with the agreement of the Court, will read. He said he was horrified, he was going to do something about it, that a commission is being set up to investigate the atrocities. Whoever did it, did it in an organised, systematic way. It was an organised group of people operating to a plan and, therefore, controlled by someone. The culprits must be identified and brought to justice, and Colonel Blaskic said he was appalled."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, Colonel Stewart came to the Hotel Vitez to bid farewell to Colonel Blaskic and to introduce his successor, Colonel Alistair Duncan, whom you also heard from in this case. This is the encounter in which Duncan attributed to Blaskic the statements that either the Serbs committed the crime in Ahmici or the BH army did it or the BH army did it dressed up as the HVO. Do Your Honours remember? I hope you do, because it was testimony that the Prosecutors read to at least a dozen other witnesses, and they said, "Colonel Duncan said that Blaskic blamed Ahmici on the Serbs or blamed it on the BH army. Wouldn't you agree that that is absurd and that he was lying?" They did that to at least twelve witnesses to try and convince Your Honours that our client is a liar, is a dishonourable man, is a deceitful man. Colonel Duncan, that was his recollection, that Colonel Blaskic said those things. Fortunately, Colonel Stewart was also present at this meeting, the 9th of May, 1993, and we asked Colonel Stewart whether this was said by Colonel Blaskic at this meeting or on any occasion, and he was very, very clear because he knew, he knew Tihomir Blaskic, he knew him well, and he remembered what Blaskic had told him about Ahmici, and this was his answer. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q In your book at page 310, you recounted a meeting with Dario Kordic in which Mr. Kordic had suggested that the Serbs had been responsible for Ahmici. Do you recall that? A I do. Q I take it you find that an incredible explanation? A Yes. I've been laughing myself sick. Q And would you agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such an explanation to you for Ahmici? A I would definitely agree that Colonel Blaskic never made such a statement to me, that the Serbs were responsible for that action."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart was at the meeting on the 9th of May, and Colonel Blaskic never made that statement, never made it to Colonel Stewart, never made it to Colonel Duncan. If you look at the testimony, on the 9th of May, there was another meeting on the 9th of May with Colonel Stewart and Colonel Duncan with Dario Kordic. The same day, the same two men met with Dario Kordic. Stewart recorded in his book, "Kordic blamed Ahmici on the Serbs," et cetera. Blaskic never, ever said that. What would those ten witnesses have said, those ten witnesses who were confronted with Duncan's accusation, how would there testimony have been charged perhaps different if their minds hadn't been polluted by this misinformation and disinformation? When a man is on trial for war crimes, it doesn't make much to inflame witnesses, to cause witnesses to truly believe that the world is black and white and that their duty is to help put this man away for the rest of his life, and if people believe that, it can affect their testimony. It certainly affects their perception and their tone. There's one other important aspect to the 9th of May meeting which I need to address. On the 4th of May, before that meeting, Colonel Stewart met with Payam Akhavan and Thomas Osorio of UNHCR, and a decision was made that although four suspects had been identified as actual direct perpetrators in the Ahmici killings, that neither the four suspects' names nor any other details would be shared with Colonel Blaskic. UNHCR insisted on that and Stewart agreed. But Stewart said he would confront Blaskic, and he did, with the fact that they had names but that they weren't going to share them with him. We know that on the 9th of May, Stewart tells Blaskic, "We have the names. We're not giving them to you. What are you going to do?" Is it any surprise that by the 10th of May, Blaskic was very impatient with the lack of demonstrable progress in the SIS investigation into Ahmici, and on the 10th of May, he issues the first written order to SIS, and he tells them to complete the investigation by the 25th of May. Two of my colleagues don't have a video monitor of this. I don't know if others do. I think we may have lost it. There we go. Thank you. So we have the 10th of May, the written order to SIS is given. This is a copy of the order. It sets a deadline for the investigation of May 25. It designates the assistant for SIS to complete the investigation. Is Blaskic papering the file, or is he reacting to what must have been a disturbing development on the 9th of May? Someone he considered he had a good working relationship with, Colonel Stewart, had told him that the International Community had names of perpetrators but they weren't sharing them with him and that Blaskic was on his own. If Blaskic ever knew, if there was a turning point where he knew there was going to be no joint investigation, that certainly was the 9th of May, when the International Community told him, "We're not sharing with you what we have. You do it yourself." Blaskic did receive a written report on the 25th of May from the SIS assistant, but it was unsatisfactory, for all the reasons that you have heard. The report was sent to Mostar as well, a copy of it. Blaskic recognised that the power and influence of the military police was potentially impeding the investigation into Ahmici, and he testified that on the 29th of May, he briefed General Petkovic and insisted that the 4th Military Police Battalion be reorganised, be subordinated to him, and that the commander, Pasko Ljubicic, be removed. Approval for this was finally received on the 4th of August, which, given the way in by bureaucracies work, was actually pretty good. In fact, Ljubicic was removed as commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion. That removal was the direct result of Colonel Blaskic's efforts. There is no evidence -- there has been no effort to show that that removal was due to any other fact or influence. Blaskic then moved forward to take full advantage of Pasko Ljubicic's removal. On the 10th of August, after getting Marinko Palavra installed as the new military police commander, he verbally instructed SIS to continue with their investigation, and on the 17th of August, he issued a second written order for an investigation. The Prosecutor faults Blaskic for waiting. There was a reason for the timing of this, and the Court, I think, understands. You must understand. I'm sure you understand, that the military police, the reorganisation of the military police, the removal of the commander that had previously lied to Blaskic about Ahmici, made possible potentially a more meaningful investigation into the Ahmici events, and Blaskic issued a second written order to take advantage of that. If you look at this order, there's something interesting, it fits in with what my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, was describing to you earlier in this argument. In paragraph 1, he orders the SIS assistant to unify all the materials and provide the bodies of district military court that are in charge with those materials. Why did he say that? Why did he want a file prepared and given to the district military court? Because it had the authority to bring criminal charges, not Blaskic. Let's face it, Ahmici was a criminal matter and is a criminal matter. Pasko Ljubicic, whom he knew, had at least covered up the crime, had been removed from his position and was shortly thereafter removed from the HVO. That is the testimony. But who the shooters were, who the arsonists were, Blaskic didn't know, he still did not know, but he was pressing and he continued to press for their identification and that that information be given to the district military court to make possible criminal prosecutions. Then he was blocked. On the 30th of September, the SIS assistant informed him that the entire report, including names, had been forwarded to the SIS administration in Mostar. When Blaskic asked for a copy of the report, the SIS assistant told him the matter was outside of his authority. The SIS administration had taken it over for reasons apparent, I think, to us all that we mentioned yesterday. We, of course, now have come full circle back to the concept of a dual line of command over the Security and Information Service in Central Bosnia. Now we do need a short private session, Your Honour, so I can explain the final piece of this chronology. utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will not go through the Operation Spider events. I would just like to mention that as a result of Operation Spider, Ivica Rajic and other members of the Maturice gang, in Kiseljak, were arrested and put on trial in Mostar. The Prosecutor, in his argument, has blamed Blaskic for the fact that apparently those individuals were acquitted by the judge or jury or Judges that heard that case. Now, Your Honours know that Blaskic had no role or powers over the prosecutors involved in those trials. Who knows what intrigue is behind those events? But the fact is it should be apparent to all that the Prosecution seeks to blame Blaskic, even for those verdicts, and that for them, Blaskic is a symbol for everything they find fault with in Herceg-Bosna and the HVO. If you look back, and I won't put it on the screen because it's not public material. If you look back at the first page of your packet, of all the entries in the timeline, all the meetings, many of which have been confirmed by international observers, all the documents, both documents that were generated at the time and that Colonel Blaskic saw and other documents that we've been able to obtain since, you have a good basis, Your Honours, to ask the question, "Was this all a ruse? Was Blaskic papering the file? Was he reacting to CNN? Or was he trying to get at the truth regarding Ahmici? We submit strongly that he wanted to know who had done this, who had misled him, who had disobeyed his orders, and who had committed this crime, but, quite frankly, from a legal perspective, Your Honours, it doesn't matter. The Prosecutor is confusing motive with intent. Why Blaskic wanted to investigate Ahmici is legally irrelevant. The fact that he did, the fact that he wanted to and the fact that he took steps, reasonable steps, under what were very difficult circumstances to do so means that he lacked the mens rea necessary to commit the crime alleged of failure to punish and failure to prevent, because motive has nothing to do with mens rea. Mens rea is intent, criminal intent. Now I return to the Vitez area, back to the 16th of April. What else happened in Vitez and what can you infer from that? You know what happened in the hamlets of Ahmici, Nadioci, Santici, and Pirici. They are all one collection of hamlets within a kilometre or two from each other. The military police were active in this entire area. Apart from that area, what actually happened in the Vitez municipality? In Kruscica, there was an armed conflict between the BH army and the HVO. The HVO and Croat residents were attacked and encircled in the Motel Lovac. There's no charge in the indictment concerning any activities in Kruscica. What about Gacice? There's no charge of any attack in Gacice on the 16th of April, no attack in Gacice on the 16th of April. The evidence is that for three days, the villagers at the local level in Gacice negotiated with each other over who would surrender weapons to the other. And on the 19th of April, those discussions broke down and there was a conflict in Gacice. What about Donja Veceriska? There was a military conflict there, and you need go no further than the statement of Midhat Haskic, one of the combatants on the Territorial Defence side, to find some of the details. There's no attack on civilians in Donja Veceriska charged in the indictment. Houses were burned, both Croat and Muslim, and that is charged, but there's no attack on civilians charged in Donja Veceriska. Where is the master plan? Why is Donja Veceriska so different from Ahmici? Why is Gacice so different from Ahmici? Why is Kruscica so different from Ahmici? In Vitez, there are attacks alleged on persons and property, and the evidence is that those attacks occurred around approximately six houses near the yellow building on the Vitez side of Stari Vitez and also by the Vitezovi -- by the Vitezovi in that area, and that also on the other side of Stari Vitez, members of Zuti's gang went to the side by the Catholic church, became involved with some fighting, lost a man or two, and may well have executed and killed one or two individuals, and we saw some pictures of, I think, a middle-aged man lying on that street by the Catholic church. Fairly small scale, sad, tragic, and criminal perhaps, but small scale events in the scheme of all the conflict, all the violence, all the fighting that was going on on the 16th, and radically and fundamentally different from what was going on in Ahmici. The Prosecution wants you to draw an inference that what happened in Ahmici and all these other places, the common thread is Blaskic because he's the commander of the territory. But if you look at what happened in these different places, you see that the common theme is local variation, local factors, local influences, events of retaliation, events of revenge, looting for personal gain. What about other municipalities? The Prosecutor said in his opening statement that on the 16th of April, there were concerted attacks in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak. What attacks occurred in the Kiseljak municipality on the morning of 16th April? None. There were none. Zero. It was later. There were attacks, there was conflict, there were battles on the 18th, based on the fact that the Vitez enclave was collapsing and there was a need to draw some of those BH forces away from Vitez. On the 16th, there were none. What about Busovaca? In the indictment, there's only one alleged attack on civilians or civilian property in the Busovaca municipality in or around April, and it's an attack that's alleged to have occurred in Ocenici. This is Ocenici if you see the small, yellow location. It's below Busovaca and it's off the main road. There was one witness who testified about Ocenici and I believe that was in open session, Mr. Nuhagic. He was a resident of this small hamlet which consisted of eight houses. There were nine families living there, and according to Mr. Nuhagic, an attack occurred on this hamlet on the 19th of April, not on the 16th. This is in the transcript at 5235. According to this same witness, the attack was by the military police, led by their commander, Pasko Ljubicic. Please check the transcript. You don't have to take my word for it. Reporter's transcript 5235. In the attack, five members of Mr. Nuhagic's family were killed, and he said in his testimony that the military police accused the residents of Ocenici of shelling them the prior day and that they came out there to exact revenge. What's the common thread, Your Honours, between the killing of civilians in Ocenici and the killing of civilians in Ahmici? Is it Colonel Blaskic or is it the 4th Battalion of the military police? What's the common thread? What's the nexus? There are no other attacks on civilians or civilian property alleged in the indictment to have occurred in Busovaca on the 16th of April. None. You have to ask yourself whether the patterns of violence support the kind of grandiose, criminal, master scheme planned and implemented by Colonel Blaskic that the Prosecutor urges or whether the world is more complex and less black and white, and if you look at the details, you see other common themes and threads that do not run to our client. There are two other incidents I wish to discuss regarding the mid April conflict in Vitez. The truck bomb and the shelling of Zenica. The truck bomb went off on 18 April on the BH army side of the front line that was encircling Stari Vitez at the time. The Prosecution alleges that Blaskic must have planned the bomb because "the explosives needed were necessarily under the control of Blaskic." Let's look at that allegation. Did Blaskic control all the explosives in Vitez? That is not what their own witnesses said. What did Captain Whitworth say about that issue? (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q The entire population of the region were armed; was it not? A Absolutely. Q Not just with small arms but there were explosives to be found among the general population, et cetera; correct? A Correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Other international observers confirmed that it was a significant problem and that the authorities in Vitez were constantly complaining of the problem that many, many private citizens had explosives. What did Charles McLeod say about this? (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Turning to the next page of this statement, did Mr. Santic also tell you that because there was an explosives factory in Vitez, I believe he said every tenth man has too much explosives or explosives in his private custody. Did he tell you that? A Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course, this is due to the fact that the SPS factory was located right next to Vitez and that it was the primary source of employment for people in Vitez. So the citizens of the area had access to the factory, and given the fear and paranoia that existed at the time, it appears that many, many citizens had their own cache of explosives, and you can be sure that Darko Kraljevic had more than a small cache of his own private explosives. He liked the big bang events, and as we saw in a BBC film, which Darko Kraljevic orchestrated, a large explosion on a hillside for BBC to record. Alternatively, the Prosecutor alleges that Blaskic must have known about the truck bomb, he must have heard about it from rumours in the town, and that he failed to prevent it. This is inconsistent with the argument that he ordered it, but, nonetheless, it's their fallback position, I suppose. If you look at Defence Exhibit D280, the Vitezovi report to the main staff, you will see that the Vitezovi regularly acted on the orders of Darko Kraljevic and not higher orders and that even when they made formal reports, they didn't send them. So if you look at that report, there's no evidence of any hand or any knowledge on the part of Colonel Blaskic in that event. What about these vague warnings? The Prosecution witnesses spoke of vague warnings, such as an explosion or something, "stay away from the window," "close your window, something is going to happen," and we heard that from three or four people. There is no evidence that such rumours reached the Operative Zone headquarters or Colonel Blaskic. If these warnings came from Vitezovi members themselves, as presumably the Prosecutor contends, then the evidence is Blaskic would have been the last person the Vitezovi would have wanted to inform of their pending attack, because Blaskic would have objected. He would have tried to stop it. What about the Zenica shelling? This has been a moving target for the Defence, if there has been one, Your Honour. In their case in chief, they contended that Bosnian Serb artillery from Mount Vlasic could not reach Zenica, and thus we knew, we all should have concluded from that that the shelling in Zenica had to be HVO. This is Major Watters. (Videotape played) "A ... from our own artillery experts that the position of his heavy-calibre artillery was not in range of Zenica. It was in range of us in Vitez but it wasn't in range of Zenica. So we deducted from that that it was, indeed, Croat artillery that had fired."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major Watters is referring to the Bosnian Serb position on Mount Vlasic as not being within range of Zenica, and you can check that. It's in the transcript at 3410. But, in fact, and we need to go into private session for just 20 seconds. In fact, this case is replete with examples --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's a big difference between west and southwest, Your Honours, a big difference. That was the proposition advanced in argument. Now, Major Baggesen did say that he thought it was a 122-millimetre shell, but the Prosecutor's witnesses could not agree on the calibre of the shell. The investigating judge entered into the official record that it was estimated to be a 155-millimetre shell, and my records reflect that this individual testified in open session, Mr. Veseljak, and so we'll hear that testimony now. (Videotape played) "A So by examining this fragment on the spot and imagining what it would look like if it was in one piece, they said that it could be a shell of 155-millimetre calibre, and that is what I entered in the record, but with the reservation that this was just an estimate."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is at transcript 5950. Then a military commission from the BH army arrived on the scene, looked at the same shell fragments, and pronounced the shell to have been 120 millimetres. This is, again, Mr. Veseljak. (Videotape played) "A ... only to be expected that they would too appear on the spot, as people responsible for military security, and I know that they did that because, while I still felt -- believed that it was 155-millimetre calibre, the military body said it was 120-millimetre calibre."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Suffice to say that what has been demonstrated is that three different people will have or, in this case, had three different opinions concerning the calibre of the shell depending on the particular fragment they picked up and based on differences in judgement. This is not a science. It is not a science. Perhaps the most significant problem, Your Honours, is that the shell fragments are gone. That's what the witnesses said. They no longer have them in the file or in the custody of the judicial authorities. The fragments were taken home by EC Monitors as souvenirs, and they're gone. The Defence had no opportunity to have them examined scientifically, the Prosecution didn't, Your Honours didn't via court witnesses or what have you. So that's the state of the record. In our case, we called Professor Jankovic, who was a ballistics engineer, and he took the calculations of Witness W, the Prosecution expert, which had been designed to show that the shell, alleged to be 122 millimetres, could have made the trip from Puticevo to Zenica, given the distance of 16 kilometres. What Professor Jankovic found was that if you took the data posited by Witness W, you found that it was mathematically impossible. If you look at the imagine before you now, these are the calculations of Professor Jankovic using the standard NATO mathematical formula, and Professor Jankovic found that the data presented by Witness W, which was designed to show that a 122-millimetre could make the trip, was mathematically impossible. In argument, the Prosecutor has responded to Professor Jankovic with the argument that, "Well, Witness W's data was wrong. He didn't have good data." So we're back at the starting point, Your Honours. The data itself with respect to direction, with respect to angle of impact, with respect to calibre of the shell, we just don't know, and that's not the stuff of a criminal case. That's not the type of evidence that anyone should be judged for individual responsible. We don't concede for a moment that even if some element within the HVO performed this shelling, we do not concede that General Blaskic ordered, condoned in any way that act, but we don't get even to that argument, Your Honours, because certainly proof beyond a reasonable doubt has not yet been established with respect to this tragedy which did occur on the 19th of April, 1993. Let's move to the Kiseljak municipality. We'll look at events in Kiseljak now from the 16th of April forward. We submit to you that Blaskic has neither direct nor command responsibility for any events in Kiseljak from the 16th of April forward for three principal reasons. He was entirely isolated and cut off from that enclave. He could not go there, other than for a few U.N. meetings, and there were only a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat your last sentence, please, Mr. Hayman? I wasn't able to grasp it quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I should slow down. I was going too fast. I will turn now to the Kiseljak municipality, to events from the 16th of April forward in that municipality. This occurred within a few weeks of the mid April conflict. Ivica Rajic returned and assumed all power in that municipality. Actually, if we go into private session for just one moment, I can identify the source of that information for Your Honours and then go back into open.
