utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The mutiny within the Kiseljak brigade only formalised what had already occurred in fact, namely, Rajic had been exercising de facto command over the brigade from outside of the formal chain of command. We know that from, among other sources, reports of international observers, such as this document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 93, which recounts, and I'll summarise it, that on the 27th of April, this is before Mijo Bozic was actually expelled because Mato Lucic was killed in early May 1993, in late April, an ECMM team is denied access to Gomionica, and the local commander denied them that access. This is the last sentence of the highlighted portion. "He stated that his commander, Ivica Rajic, had given orders to stop all U.N., UNHCR, and ECMM vehicles." So we know that even before Rajic replaced Bozic, Rajic is giving orders contrary to Colonel Blaskic's orders, in this case, for example, to block access by international observers. It is clear from the evidence that Blaskic had no ability to control Rajic. Rajic was a ruthless figure who used violence to consolidate his power within the HVO, and I would like you to hear Ed Vulliamy's description of Rajic's take-over, violent take-over of the Vares HVO, consolidating his own personal power. (Videotape played) "A ... I should have added to the list was included Travnik and Tuzla. But in Vares, something very sad happened. In Vares, which is just above Olovo in the eastern bit of Central Bosnia, the HVO was again wanting to be cooperative with the Bosnian government army, and they were themselves deposed during 1993 by other units of the HVO who came up from Kiseljak to depose, get rid of, the elements in the HVO who had sought to cooperate with the Bosnian army. Q And those were the forces and units of Ivica Rajic that came up from Kiseljak -- A That's right. Q -- and had effective control over Vares; correct? A That's right."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The Court may recall from other evidence in the case that Rajic perfected his control in Vares through the murder also of the SIS assistant in Vares, Duznovic. He was murdered by Rajic, thus eliminating the dual line of control of command in Vares, placing Rajic solely in control in Vares, and he similarly consolidated his control and power in the Kiseljak municipality. Blaskic, isolated in Vitez, had no chance to effect control over a man committed to such tactics and exercising such powers. My third and last point on Kiseljak is that the HVO main staff had a command relationship over the Kiseljak HVO that was direct, that is, a line of command and communications went directly from the main staff in Mostar to Kiseljak. Now, why was that the case? Among other reasons, that's because the main staff could physically visit the Kiseljak municipality through Bosnian Serb territory, and they did on a regular basis, and General Petkovic did on a regular basis, and that is in the evidence of this case. Indeed, the evidence is that the main staff actually had a forward command post in Kiseljak. The evidence is also that the HVO liaison officer in the Kiseljak municipality, this is a man named Vinko Lucic, he reported to Mostar. He was a liaison officer from Mostar in Kiseljak reporting directly to Mostar, not to the Operative Zone, and the Canadian Battalion, who were responsible for this area, confirmed that, and I'd like to point your direction to Captain Lanthier's testimony in this regard. (Videotape played) "Judge Riad: What was the exact position of -- what was his exact responsibility? In relation to General Blaskic, what was Vinko Lucic? A I had been introduced to him as -- he himself introduced himself as the liaison officer of the HVO army headquarters in Mostar, and he answered to the Mostar headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That means, Your Honours, that complaints by international agencies to the liaison officer in Kiseljak went to the main staff, not to Colonel Blaskic. He should not go to gaol for life, as the Prosecutor requests, for such matters that were not even reported to him but were reported directly to his commanders in Mostar. Lastly, I would point you to an order from General Petkovic, which he sent in August of 1993 -- or a request, it's not even an order, but it's a request which, plainly on its face, is being sent to two equals. It reads: "Preparing of actions. For Tiho and Rajic. Act urgently on coordination," et cetera, et cetera, "Signed, Milivoj Petkovic." Now, I ask you, Your Honours, is this an order to equals, "Tiho and Rajic," or is this an order to a superior officer at the Operative Zone level and an inferior officer at the brigade or even the Operative Group level? This quite plainly is a communication to de facto equals in recognition of the fact that Rajic was in direct command under the main staff of the Kiseljak HVO. Now, there's one particular incident in Kiseljak I do want to talk about it in greater detail. I won't talk about the others, Rotilj, and other terrible things that happened in Tulica and some of the other villages, but I do want to talk about Gomionica. There was an attack on the 18th of April in Gomionica by the Kiseljak HVO, and this, we believe, is important. It illustrates many things, but also it is cited in the Prosecutor's final brief, in book 7, part 12, section 2.193, as an illegal order by Blaskic. They call it an order "to ethnically cleanse the villages" of Gomionica and Svinjarevo. That is how it is characterised in their final brief. What does this order, Defence Exhibit 299, say? It's dated the 17th of April, and I'd like to show you a portion of it. It tells the Kiseljak Brigade to prepare to launch a combat activity against Gomionica and Svinjarevo for the purpose of reducing pressure on the Vitez enclave, and Colonel Blaskic told the Kiseljak HVO exactly how to launch this attack. He told them, "Take control of Gomionica and Svinjarevo, and the principal movement of forces should be to attack in groups and only diagonally from locations called Kocatale and Sikulja." The quote actually is: "The attack of the main forces is to be from Sikulja ..." and so forth. By the way, I note there's an error on the second line here. This order -- first and second line. This is actually, I'm referring to D299, which is an order from the morning of the 17th of April. It's a preparatory combat order, and we have the French of this same order. So this is an order to take control of Gomionica and Svinjarevo by proceeding with the main forces from the two locations I named towards the high ground above Gomionica. Now, you may recall General Blaskic described this order in his testimony, and he drew a handdrawn map, which you now see on the screens in front of you. Actually, I need to go back. If you will just bear with me for a moment. There's another location referenced in one of the orders Hadrovci, and that is actually the other location that we have identified on this map, which he identified and will subsequently be identified in another map that I'm going to show you in a moment. The point is that at the bottom of this diagram, you have the main road, then you have the village on the slope of the hill, you have a feature high above the village, and you have two other features along a ridge next to the high feature. Here's a little bit more of a better map. You can see the main road runs between Gomionica and Gromiljak from the upper left of the map running down towards the middle of the bottom of the map, and you can see on the map, we haven't added the names on the map, we've simply added the arrows, you can see the high ground and that the order was to take control of Svinjarevo and Gomionica by taking control of the high ground. Because once the high ground was secured, Gomionica and Svinjarevo would be cut off from Visoko, which is where the 1st Corps was. There was a road running between the two that the BH army had built. Once you cut them off, you have effective control, and you can do it in a very efficient and military-precise manner. The purpose of this -- well, the military objective is obvious because Gomionica was the headquarters of the BH army in the Kiseljak municipality, and there was a large detachment there, but the purpose of ordering the attack in this way, which Blaskic did, was to avoid combat in a built-up area and avoid unnecessary destruction to civilian structures or risk to civilian lives. What happened was the Kiseljak Brigade apparently attacked Gomionica from the main road and got mired in combat in the village itself, which is reflected in the very meagre reports that General Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic, received. In this report, all they say is: "We have lost Zavrtaljka," which is the high feature to the northwest of Gomionica and which dominates the road from Kiseljak to Bilalovac, and it says: "We did not manage to handle Gomionica, but we did take around one kilometres on both sides around Gomionica," which is not the objective, is not how Colonel Blaskic had ordered the Kiseljak Brigade to proceed. It's also interesting, Your Honours, that this act, this action was to begin early on the morning of the 18th of April, and if you look at the time when this report was actually received in Vitez, it's received at 17.13, the end of the day, some ten hours perhaps after the combat action had actually commenced. So I wanted to speak specifically to that order and that action, Your Honours, because it illustrates the command and control difficulties that Blaskic had with respect to Kiseljak and also because the Prosecutor has claimed in their brief that this was an illegal order, and we think that it is not the case. Now I will talk about events after mid April. There are, of course, many other things that we can say about April, and they're in our final briefs, but there is no need to recount them all. That's not the purpose of final argument in a case like this with so many facts and details. I will address the attack on Stari Vitez on the 18th of July, 1993 and then the Grbavica battle in September. With respect to the Stari Vitez attack, it is our position that Blaskic neither ordered nor knew about the attack while it was occurring, nor was he informed after the fact that the attack violated international law, and it is our position that the attack did not violate international law, and thus even if he knew about it or in some way failed to prevent it, no criminal liability can attach. As background, I'd like to refresh your memories about Stari Vitez for a moment. What was Stari Vitez? It was defended by an organised military force numbering approximately 250 defenders. This is Sefkija Dzidic. (Videotape played) "Q Can you tell me, if we include the military and civilian police, how many troops did you have at your disposal during these eleven months of siege? A Between 200 and 250 men."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So we have 250 soldiers in Stari Vitez, according to Major Hunter, at transcript page 5100. They were armed with 60 millimetre mortars, rocket-propelled grenades, sniper rifles, and other small arms, and according to Sefkija Dzidic himself, at 1455, Stari Vitez was heavily fortified on all sides and throughout. Indeed, as Major Hunter confirmed, Stari Vitez, it was a threat, a military threat to Vitez, and it was a location of military significance in this conflict. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Would you agree that the presence of the BH army in Stari Vitez was of military significance to both warring parties? A Yes, clearly it was ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would also suggest to the Court, urge, that it is clear from the evidence that the HVO did take steps to alleviate the conditions that civilians in Stari Vitez suffered under, as did, by the way, many of the same conditions were suffered under by the civilians in Vitez. Adequate food was allowed into Stari Vitez. The HVO, on several occasions, offered civilians the opportunity to temporarily leave Stari Vitez in order to escape the war zone, and liaison officer Captain Whitworth confirmed that for Your Honours. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q During your tour of duty, did you become familiar with the offers made by the Croat community in Vitez to the citizens of Stari Vitez to temporarily evacuate Stari Vitez and get out of the war zone? A Yes, I was aware of those offers."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Military and civilian targets were also blurred in Stari Vitez. Now, what do I mean by that? What I mean by that is that military structures, military personnel, weapons, logistics, all these things occurred, were stored, were deployed in structures that weren't dedicated to a military purpose or marked with a military marking. They were ordinary structures, civilian structures. Indeed, it has been testified in this case that everyone was active in the defence of Stari Vitez, men and women. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q And were all such males in Stari Vitez active in the military defence of Stari Vitez? A Everybody was active in the defence of Stari Vitez. Q You're saying men and women were active in the defence? A I saw women bearing arms as well, if they were of that ilk."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What that means when military and civilian targets are blurred is that it is more difficult for any military force, seeking to take action against that legitimate military target, to separate the military and civilian targets and to reduce potential damage to civilian structures and harm to civilians. Now, what do we know about HVO actions with respect to Stari Vitez? You have heard that calls for an all-out attack on Stari Vitez mounted as civilian casualties in Vitez mounted into the summer of 1993. Captain Bower described that at 9451. Captain Bower also told this Court that Blaskic resisted such calls, he would not allow artillery to be used, and that the HVO strategy in the main was simply to try and contain the BH army in Stari Vitez and prevent them from breaking out, Captain Bower at 9386. Indeed, it was widely known and resented by the Croat community in Vitez that Blaskic would not allow artillery to be used against Stari Vitez, protected witness at transcript page 17716. We also urge Your Honours to consider with great caution the testimony of Sefkija Dzidic, who was the Prosecutor's main witness to testify about the siege and any attacks on Stari Vitez. Why? Because he was not candid with this Court. I remind Your Honours of his testimony that he flatly denied that any arms were transported by UNPROFOR forces into Stari Vitez. (Videotape played) "Mr. Nobilo: Q Throughout 11 months, a lot of it was used up. How did you refill it? A We got new ammunition from captives, and we took the ammunition people had in houses. Q Did the UNPROFOR bring in any ammunition and military equipment? A No, never."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But UNPROFOR officers testified in this case too, and one of those officers, Captain Whitworth again, testified concerning the smuggling of munitions into Stari Vitez personally by Sefkija Dzidic. Here is his testimony. He also confronted Dzidic after the event, although I don't recall if it's in the clip as well. This is at transcript page 10254. (Videotape played) "A I'd been asked to take some medical supplies into Stari Vitez and picked up several small boxes of medical supplies from the UNHCR building in Zenica, which was a Muslim enclave, took them into Stari Vitez, handed them over to Commander Sefkija. He immediately handed them over to one of his subordinates who took them away to another room. I sat and drank coffee and exchanged pleasantries of the day, assessing the situation with Commander Sefkija. And then shortly after it was decided, I made the excuse to leave and took a walk around the houses and buildings adjacent to Commander Sefkija's headquarters. I walked into a room and found them unpacking the boxes that were allegedly full of bandages, and inside each of the bandages was a box of 20 rounds of ammunition. So there was maybe 600, 1.000 rounds in total, that if each box had contained, you know, 400 or 500 rounds, so they'd managed to wrap a carton of 20 rounds in a bandage basically and then stick a box full of bandages in the back of my vehicle."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I recall myself, from Captain Whitworth's testimony, that Captain Whitworth testified that he then confronted Sefkija Dzidic with the fact that it was wrong to use UNHCR aid and UNPROFOR to smuggle weapons in, and Dzidic shrugged his shoulders and said, "It's necessary." That's what Dzidic said. By the way, I don't mean to pick up Dzidic. They had problems. They needed munitions. So be it. But we're simply identifying for Your Honours that you need to scrutinise testimony like that with care because these are people, such as Mr. Dzidic, he suffered greatly in the war, he had a terrible position, being isolated in Stari Vitez for ten months, just like those in the Vitez pocket were isolated, and that kind of testimony, in light of these contradictions, must be carefully scrutinised. Now let's turn to the 18th of July attack. There is no evidence that Blaskic ordered the attack or knew about it in advance. In fact, if you look at the Vitezovi report to the main staff, D250, it states that there was an order from the commander of the Vitezovi, and that was the order to attack Stari Vitez on the 18th of July. There's no reference to any order from Colonel Blaskic. In fact, witnesses testified that the attack was planned and instigated by Kraljevic in retaliation for an attack by the BH army on Kraljevic's brother a day or two earlier. That's in the transcript. A protected witness testified to that effect at 17715. Now, the attack itself, the 18th of July, 1993, was on a Sunday. You can check the calendar, and please take judicial notice of that, but the calendar in 1993 was actually aligned with this year's calendar. So if you look at this year's calendar, you will see that the 16th of April is a Friday and that the 18th of July this year is also -- or, rather, was on a Sunday. Colonel Blaskic testified, then Colonel Blaskic, that he was in Busovaca on the 18th of July. He attended church, he had lunch with the parish priest, who was a good friend of his, and that he had gone the prior evening to Busovaca to spend what part of the weekend he could get away for there, and he did not return to Vitez until after the attack apparently had concluded. By the way, it ended in a complete debacle for the Vitezovi with a large number of dead and wounded soldiers. Now, I'll come back to that weekend visit to Busovaca, but first I'd like to respond to the argument that the Prosecution made in their argument, that this was not a Vitezovi attack, it was really an HVO attack, and they rely on documents which purportedly reflect that HVO soldiers in other units sustained injuries on the 18th of July in the vicinity. It is important to remember, Your Honours, that the front line around Stari Vitez was manned by Vitez Brigade militia. They were there from the 16th of April on, and they were there on the 18th of July. Someone had to man the front line. That was not the Vitezovi. They did not view that as their task. So when the Vitezovi came and they launched their attack, and the BH army responded very effectively from Stari Vitez with heavy fire, casualties were sustained along that front line. That's normal and to be expected. Now, what about the Prosecutor's documents? What do they really show? One of those documents was P758, and if you look at that document, and they offered this again to show that a soldier was wounded on Stari Vitez who was not a member of the Vitezovi but was actually a member of a regular HVO brigade, if you look at this document, you'll see that it's dated in 1994. The Vitezovi no longer existed in 1994, and the document doesn't reflect what unit this individual belonged to in 1993. The next document they offered, 759, indicates that an individual, killed on the 18th of July, was mobilised on the 16th of April into the HVO and was killed by a counterattack on the defensive line around Stari Vitez. As I said, that's exactly what one would expect. But there's something else that's very interesting about this document, Your Honours, this is P759. Look who signed this document. This is a document from the 92nd Brigade, the 92nd Brigade of the HVO, certifying that a certain soldier was killed on the 18th of July. Look who signed this as commander or deputy commander of the 92nd Regiment of the HVO: Dragan Vinac. If you see that name, this is the signature line enlarged. Who is Dragan Vinac? Well, apparently in 1994, which I think is the date of this article, he has some command position in the 92nd Regiment of the HVO. But look at D250, the report of the Vitezovi. Who signed that report as deputy commander of the Vitezovi in late 1993 -- I guess early 1994? The other document is later in 1994. Dragan Vinac. Let's look at those two signatures again, if you will. Here's Dragan Vinac signing as a commander in the 92nd Regiment, late in 1996, actually, Your Honours, if you look at the top. That's January 1996. Here's D250, in February of 1994, Dragan Vinac signing as commander of the Vitezovi. So what does that tell you? That tells you that you cannot infer from these documents, these documents from 1994, 1995, 1996, what unit these people belonged to in 1993. The man signing these documents for the 92nd Regiment was the deputy commander of the Vitezovi in 1993 and at least up until February of 1994. Now to return to Tihomir Blaskic's weekend plans on the 17th and 18th of July, 1993. The Prosecutor claims Blaskic lied, he never left Vitez on that weekend. I would ask you to think about what you know about his routine, think back to late January 1993, when he left Vitez on a Saturday afternoon, January 23rd, to go visit his family home in Brestovsko for the balance of the weekend. He got cut off on that weekend visit and was stuck in Kiseljak on the 25th of January and beyond. The Prosecution finds it incredible that he did a similar thing on Saturday, the 17th of July, although, of course, by then he couldn't go home to his parents in Brestovsko, he was cut off, so he testified that he went to Busovaca to visit his good friend, the parish priest. Is it incredible that he tried to get away for the tail end of Saturday and the first two-thirds or so of Sunday, the 18th of July? Or is it perfectly normal that he would try to get away for at least one day of the weekend? You will recall that he was not a native of Vitez. He didn't even have an apartment there. He lived in his office. He had a bunk, and this was described to you by witnesses, in the back of his office with his chairs and his desk. He had a small bunkbed and a little screen, and that is where he lived in Vitez. He did not have a flat in Vitez. Sitting in your office all weekend is not very pleasant. It's something that all the lawyers in this case hope to do less of in the near future, but even during the war, when it wasn't absolutely necessary, due to combat conditions that were known and expected, it's perfectly natural to expect Blaskic to want to try and get away for a weekend day, and it's normal for someone who's not a native, who doesn't have family in the area, to try and do that. We've all tried to do that from time to time during this trial, those of us who are visitors here in The Hague. We're creatures of habit, and sometimes our habits become known to others, and others can take advantage of that knowledge, and we submit to you that is what Darko Kraljevic did on the 18th of July, when he planned and executed a surprise attack on Stari Vitez. Now, our last contention with respect to the attack on Stari Vitez is that it did not violate international law. That has not been proven. It seems to be assumed but it has not been proven. The charge is that the attack was indiscriminate and that hundreds of "babies" showered down on Stari Vitez and that it caused disproportionate death and destruction to civilian structures and the civilian population. If you look at the U.N. report on this attack, P710, you will see several things about this attack. It says: "No artillery was used. Only mortars and RPGs." It says, "Mainly RPGs, and 60/80/120 mortars" were used. Those are infantry weapons not artillery. There is also no report of the use of "babies." The milinfosum does not report any use of "babies." Indeed, the liaison officer at the time, Captain Whitworth, said he never saw a "baby," this is a "baby," the fire extinguisher, an improvised home-made explosive devices. He never saw one fired on Stari Vitez; that's at the transcript page 10382. So prove the attack was illegal, the Prosecution must prove disproportionate civilian casualties or disproportionate destruction to civilian structures, vis-à-vis relative to the attack. Captain Bower of BritBat testified very specifically as to what the casualties were. There was one man of military age, in his 40s, apparently fit, who was killed in the attack. There's no information whether he was a soldier or a civilian, but there certainly is a strong inference that he was the former. And sadly, there was one woman and one child who were wounded and evacuated. That's a total of three civilian casualties. That's in the transcript at 9384, and the Prosecution concedes in their final brief that there were only three casualties, that's in book 5, page 181. So we know there were a total of three casualties, assume they're all civilian, three casualties. There were between 1.600 and 2.000 people in Stari Vitez, at least 250 full-time soldiers, and we ask you, for a major assault in a built-up area lasting the better part of eight, ten hours, are three civilian casualties, is that disproportionate for a major military action against what was a legitimate military target? Three civilian casualties, one death. We submit that is per se not disproportionate. Any casualties are unfortunate and tragic for those involved, but three casualties with respect to such an attack is per se not disproportionate. How many civilian structures were destroyed in the attack? There's no reference to any destruction of civilian structures in the U.N. report. The evidence, in fact, is that Stari Vitez was heavily fortified and that structures, in any event, were used for defence, for storing defence materials, and the like. So we submit, even if you assume that General Blaskic learned that an attack in Stari Vitez was ongoing, there was nothing illegal about that attack. Now I turn to the Grbavica battle. After mid April, there are only these two alleged crimes in the Vitez enclave, only two events after mid April in the Vitez municipality. We asked you to consider, were things getting better? Was Blaskic able to build a better system of command and control, as we move on from April? We have two alleged crimes from late April 1993 until January of 1994, only two. Compare that to all the carnage and all the problems in April. That tells us something, Your Honours, I submit. Grbavica. The charge is destruction and plunder of property in Grbavica in September of 1993. There is no charge of any unlawful attack on civilians in Grbavica, and that is because there were no civilian casualties in Grbavica. The Prosecution concedes that the attack complied with military necessity, and they assert that the crime consisted of the unnecessary burning of civilian structures during the battle and the burning and looting of civilian structures or any structure after the battle was concluded. First of all, with respect to the battle itself, we asked you to consider that there was house-to-house fighting, heavy house-to-house fighting in Grbavica, and the houses in Grbavica were used by the BH army as defensive positions. This is Captain Bower. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q How did the BH army defend this line, the blue-dotted line? Where were their positions and where were they firing from? A I can't give any great details as to where individuals were. The bulk of their defensive positions were on the high ground, but they did use the houses as cover to fight from."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So what happened is the BH army moved up the hill and retreated to the top of the feature. They used the houses along the way for defence, for defensive cover, and the testimony in this case is when you're trying to clear a military unit out of a built-up area, you destroy the houses if you can and you use any means you can. That is normal, expected, legitimate military tactics. It is a tribute to the HVO that they were able to complete that action with no civilian deaths. It is a tribute to Colonel Blaskic, then Colonel Blaskic, that he was able to accomplish that. But it is normal and it should be expected that some houses would be damaged, perhaps destroyed, perhaps burned as a result of explosions, grenades, and incendiary fire, and once one house catches fire, Your Honours, in this kind of a built-up area, does the fire brigade come out and put it out in the middle of a battle? No. Fires can spread under these conditions. We don't know if this happened. We don't know exactly what happened because the BritBat observers were taking cover. They weren't watching the battle on any kind of continuous basis. What we heard is that Captain Whitworth left the area for about two hours in the middle of the day, he went to the Hotel Vitez, he had his conversation with Darko Gelic, and when he returned, about two hours after noon, he saw some houses on fire, and there is a photograph, although it is gone now, I hoped it would still be in a courtroom, it shows a line, a trees, some ridge, and it shows some smoke above the ridge. Is that smoke from two houses burning or five or six? And whether it's two or five or six or even ten houses burning during the battle, is that to be -- is that unexpected? There are over a hundred houses on that hill, on that feature. It is not known how many BH army full-time structures there were, headquarters, munitions, logistics, and so forth. Did the BH army burn their archive, set fire to their headquarters, before they pulled out? That would be normal. You don't want the other side catching your archives, all your confidential papers, or your equipment and so forth. Nobody from the BH army testified on those subjects. As I said, we know that despite two days of fighting in a built-up area, there was not a civilian casualty. (Videotape played) "Judge Riad: What happened? A Here, I don't think we found any civilian casualties."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That was Captain Whitworth at transcript page 10272. He's talking about the whole area, the whole battle, although sometimes we don't play the whole segment to save time. The photographs of a burned and gutted village, Your Honours, that the Prosecution has shown regarding Grbavica were taken in 1997. That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 447, and they admitted as much when they tendered them. But there aren't any photographs depicting the situation in the village with respect to how many houses had been damaged. During the afternoon of the 8th of September, the second day of the battle. What we do know is that the BBC was there and that they reported that the burning and looting in Grbavica occurred that evening, at least by late afternoon, and Captain Whitworth confirmed that, because we viewed the BBC tape. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q The BBC tape then says that looting and burning occurred later on in the night time. Do you agree with that? A Yes. I think, as I said yesterday, there were numerous vehicles -- lorries turned up."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about looting? The Prosecution must be arguing that there was systematic or organised looting in Grbavica, because if you're talking about command responsibility, you can't attribute command responsibility to one or two soldiers taking a radio or an axe. This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 433-24; purported looting in Grbavica. And you can see there are two men in uniform. One is carrying either a briefcase or a boombox radio, and one appears to be carrying some kind of a meat cleaver. There are no other photos or specific descriptions of any looting by soldiers in Grbavica. And I ask you, Your Honours. You see a soldier carrying something in an area like this, it raises a question in my mind: How much military equipment was there in the BH army military structures in the area? They occupied the area for a long period of time. There was a battalion headquarters down along the road, Major Hunter described that. There were other structures. How much equipment, foodstuffs, were in those structures? How many trucks would it have taken to even haul that stuff away, which the HVO would have been entitled to seize as ordinary military activity? The Prosecutor makes no attempt to distinguish between what is truly legitimate military activity or individual acts of radio theft versus some kind of systematic looting by military units or by a large number of soldiers. There's just no evidence of any systematic looting by soldiers. What the evidence is is that the battle ended by mid afternoon and the front line moved forward, and this is important when we get to the detention crimes and alleged trench-digging crimes, the front line moved off of Grbavica, and the civil police came in to secure the area and search the area for any dangerous items, like mines, bombs, hidden devices, and Defence Exhibit 582 is the report of the commander of the civil police in Vitez indicating that on the afternoon of the 8th, indeed, they moved in, and they did a search, a search and securing of the location. But what else did you hear from the witnesses? The testimony from the international observers was that what happened was destitute refugees from all over the Lasva Valley, and there were tens of thousands of these people there, they came after the battle to Grbavica, and they scavenged, and they even ripped the wood frames out of the windows and the doors to use for firewood. Why would they do that? This was September. Winter was coming. These people had nothing. They came to Grbavica, these refugees, to strip the wood out of the window sills, off the doors, and Captain Whitworth confirmed this for you. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Did you see whether the locals who descended on Grbavica on the 8th to loot, et cetera, what was their state, or could you tell? A They just seemed to be coming down scavenging and looting for whatever there could be. They were people from as far up the valley as Nova Bila, the Novi Travnik area."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That passage is at transcript page 10419, and Captain Whitworth is not talking about soldiers. He is talking about truckloads of destitute refugees that descended on Grbavica and started to strip the window frames and anything else they could take out of these structures. The civil police were overwhelmed. In fact, reports are one scavenger was shot dead, and then the civil police backed off. Even if Your Honours found a crime at Grbavica for which Tihomir Blaskic should be held accountable, we submit there's no evidence that anyone informed him that soldiers had committed a crime at Grbavica. Captain Whitworth testified that after his noon visit, which was still during the battle, no other information, no other protest was ever made to the Hotel Vitez operative command, Operative Zone command. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Was any other protest or expression of concern made other then your noon on the 8th visit to the Hotel Vitez, to your knowledge? A There was no point, as far as I was concerned. The battle was over and done. The HVO had claimed Grbavica, and the Muslim population had withdrawn. Q The answer is no? A The answer is no."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Major Hunter testified. He never told Blaskic that they thought this was a crime by HVO soldiers. Captain Bower testified. He never said they told Blaskic this was a crime by HVO soldiers. Alistair Duncan testified. He never told Blaskic this was a crime by HVO soldiers. In fact, the only evidence is that BritBat congratulated Blaskic on a professional battle, a battle he won, and a battle he won with no civilian casualties. Your Honours, at this time, my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, will speak, I believe, on the subject of international armed conflict, and then when he is concluded, and he will carry over after the luncheon hour, I would like to address detention crimes and forcible transfer, detention crimes, forcible transfer, religious objects, and one or two other short categories, and then, Your Honour, this trial will be over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you wish to begin for the ten minutes we have? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, because we are short of time anyway, so we must make the best of every minute we have. As you heard, in accordance with our division of labour between the two of us, I will be speaking to you about the possibility of the implementation of Article 2 of the Statute of the International Tribunal in The Hague, and the possible responsibility based on that provision of General Blaskic. The Prosecution, in counts 5, 8, 11, 15, 17, and 19, have charged General Blaskic of committing crimes pursuant to Article 2 of the Statute of the International Tribunal. For General Blaskic to be liable for those acts, it has to be proven that in Bosnia, in the critical period and in the period in question, there was an international conflict and that the victims were protected persons, that they had the status of protected persons under the 1949 Geneva Conventions and, of course, that such criminal offences actually occurred. By way of introduction, I should like to say that the International Red Cross, on the 22nd of May, 1992, brought together representatives of the three peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, their parties, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, the Muslim, Serb, and Croat parties, and that organised by the International Red Cross, they agreed to sign an agreement recognising that what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina was an internal armed conflict. These were political parties, and they were not binding on any state or military structure, but I think that it is important to note that the International Red Cross believed at the time and that the representatives of all three nations could conclude from that that, indeed, there was an internal armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As I said, for us to be able to apply Article 2 of the Statute, apart from a concrete crime, the protected character of civilians has to be proven and the existence of an international conflict. In this particular case, the Prosecution has to prove that the HVO, which was, in fact, fighting in Central Bosnia, was an agent of the Republic of Croatia. For that agency relationship to be proven, in accordance with the judgement of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case, the Prosecution has to prove that Croatia or the Croatian army had general control, coordination, and supervision over the Croatian Defence Council. Numerous factors and tests were recognised by the Tadic Chamber in their decision which can be helpful in establishing whether there was an international conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Croats and the Serbs. So we can make a comparison. The control tests made in the Tadic appeals judgement regarding the army of the Republika Srpska and the BH army can also be applied to the conflict between the HVO and the BH army. Whether the positions adopted by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case can also apply to the conflict between the HVO and the BH army, and can it be treated as an international armed conflict? One of the first elements which was highlighted with emphasis by the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case is that the army of Republika Srpska was a fictitious structure, that it was, in fact, a transformed Yugoslav people's party. We know from before and from this trial that the JNA had withdrawn from Croatia and that it had existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout, and at one point in time, they simply said, "We are no longer the JNA; we are the army of Republika Srpska," but the same troops and organisation remained. Let us try to apply this same test to the HVO and Croatian army. The HVO is an autochthonous organisation. We have seen that it was formed out of local villagers. No Croatian armies came to Bosnia and stated, "We are no longer the Croatian army; we are now the HVO." We saw the painstaking efforts General Blaskic made to build an army out of untrained peasants. Furthermore, the HVO, which we shall be coming back to later on to show that it was an allied force in relation to the BH army, but let me just state that the army of Republika Srpska never had the recognised status by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a legitimate armed force. Let me remind you of the agreement between the HVO and the BH army of the 20th of April in Zenica, when General Halilovic and Petkovic were present. Halilovic was chief of staff of the BH army, and that agreement explicitly states that the HVO is one component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina the second component. Thus, in those initial documents that we are reviewing, we already see a substantive difference between the army of Republika Srpska and the HVO. The Prosecution asserts that the HVO shared the same goals as the Republic of Croatia. Again, by way of introduction, I would like to say that according to the position taken by the Tadic Appeals Chamber, that is, in itself, not sufficient to prove the existence of overall control of the Republic of Croatia over the HVO. The Prosecution claims that Franjo Tudjman had this idea to divide Bosnia, that through Boban, Kordic, Kostroman, and Valenta, he transposed that idea into Bosnia-Herzegovina and that Blaskic was an instrument of that idea. Even though that is not sufficient, let us examine what the grounds are for the Prosecution's conclusion that the Republic of Croatia was acting with a view to dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let us see whether there is a single piece of evidence to prove that that is the direction in which Croatia was acting. Mr. President, we should now go into private session, and it's only about half a minute to one, so I propose we have our lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Prosecution sent quite a bit of time in proving that the idea of President Tudjman was a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would be a hostile policy towards this state, and the key thesis, which invokes the support, was the meeting in Karadjordjevo on the 30th of March, 1991 between Presidents Tudjman and Milosevic. Allegedly, it is there that the division of Bosnia was agreed upon. It is something that was speculated on in the media, it was something that was rumoured, it was something that was whispered about, but, Your Honours, before you, no single shred of evidence was presented on what were the contents of this meeting and what decisions were taken there. So we have no witness, we have no document which would show what the contents of the meetings in Karadjordjevo were and what decisions were taken. We can judge on Karadjordjevo only on the basis of the consequences of this meeting, and we have to place it in the context of time. That was the 30th of March, 1991. At that time, the conflicts had already started in Croatia, but they had not escalated at that time. At that time, the rebel Serbs were active in Croatia, which assisted the JNA which used them as an instrument and it was arming them. President Tudjman was trying to prevent a war, and in the context of this effort to prevent a war, this meeting in Karadjordjevo should be viewed. Now, if what the Prosecution claims is true, that is, that there was an agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic in Karadjordjevo, then the question arises: How come that after Karadjordjevo, after the 30th of March of 1991, the real war in Croatia only began? It was after the 30th of March that the city of Vukovar was attacked and completely destroyed. This was a city in Croatia. And also the city of Dubrovnik, a Croatian coastal town. How can it be that the partners, after having reached an agreement, are starting a real war in earnest? This is another piece of evidence that this agreement never took. Or it was said that Milosevic and Tudjman were partners because they had reached an agreement. What type of agreement is this that if, after Karadjordjevo, a JN plane flew to Zagreb and bombed the offices of President Tudjman? Ten minutes before this attack, he went to a restaurant with Stipo Mesic and Ante Markovic, the last prime minister, they went to a restaurant ten minutes before that. So it is clear that there was no agreement. How would you also explain that General Bobetko entered Bosnia to prevent the JNA from taking full control of Bosnia at that time? So the war really only started after Karadjordjevo, and the only thing we can conclude is that there was no agreement. We do not know what the contents of this meeting were. We do not know whether there was an effort to come to an agreement, but we know the consequences, what happened after Karadjordjevo. It is true that President Tudjman, on several occasions, both publically and privately, advocated a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is true. That is correct. It is true that in 1981, Mr. Tudjman, as a historian, wrote that Bosnia should be divided. However, what the Prosecution did was manipulate this, that is, taking these true statements, and they turned it into a thesis and say, "The Republic of Croatia advocated the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina," but there is no evidence that the Republic of Croatia advocated the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. President Tudjman is the president of the Republic of Croatia, but the policy of the Republic of Croatia is reflected in documents, open documents, official documents, such as laws, decrees, and in the actual steps, measures taken by the Republic of Croatia. So that is how its real position is reflected. In creation of an international policy, it is clear that leadership plays a significant role, but as this international or foreign policy is being created in the bodies of the state, you have to take into account both the internal and foreign relations. Croatia is a small country, and you have to take into account all the influences and positions that you have. A real politician has to take into account all the different factors. Let's say that the aim may be or the desire may be to, let's say, divide the country, but the real policy prevents you from actually pursuing such a policy. I will just mention a couple of things, but most importantly, there is no shred of evidence that the policy of the Republic of Croatia was going in the direction of division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How are we to reconcile this policy with the fact that the Republic of Croatia was the first state to have recognised the existence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as early as April 7, 1992? And on 19 April, 1992, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina signed an agreement on the diplomatic councillor missions abroad, and the Republic of Croatia undertakes to protect the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina, interests in those countries where Bosnia did not have its own diplomatic missions. The ambassadors were exchanged in 1992 and early 1993. On 19 January, 1993, the first ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived in Zagreb, and before that, the Croatian ambassador was already in Sarajevo. Also, on 14 June, 1993, President Tudjman visited Sarajevo, and throughout this period, they never interrupted their diplomatic ties. The Croatian parliament adopted at least two declarations: One is D106 of 30 April, 1993. In this declaration of the Croatian parliament, Croatia says: "The historic friendship of Croats and Muslims is a prerequisite for the surcivil of both of these people in this region. It is the foundation for sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its future." This is the declaration of the Croatian parliament which speaks about the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also, Exhibit D107 of 30 June, 1993 where Croatia supports the internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, its sovereignty, and territorial integrity. So much on that issue, and we will further argue that these two countries were allies throughout. But now regarding the general control of the HV over the HVO or the Republic of Croatia over the HVO. A series of exhibits were introduced regarding Bobetko's orders. We got them as a series. But if you look at them, what are their dates? 16 April, 17 May, 20 April, all 1992. 21 and 22 April 1992. In other words, all proofs which points to the fact that the HV controlled the HVO. All of these documents are from a period between April and May 1992, and we know that Bobetko was in Bosnia-Herzegovina until July of 1992. However, we must take into account the situation which was there at the time. The HVO in April, May, in June of 1992 did not even exist. It was formally established on 8 April, 1992, but only on 3 July, 1992, a law was adopted which provided a foundation for the HVO. What was in this interim period? What existed then? Also, formally, a main staff was established, and there were municipal staffs, but not as military bodies. But in these military staffs, there were politicians who were working on preparation for a military defence, and also there were villages which had armed groups. That was all. Even Tihomir Blaskic, when he was named on 27 June, 1992, was not appointed commander of an operative zone, so not an already established organisation, but as a commander of a regional staff which was unifying local municipal staffs in the area of Central Bosnia. These were civilian military bodies which were working on the preparations, logistics works, and so on, for the defence. There was no HVO at that time. In the Aleksovski case and in the Tadic case, I think it is clearly stated that we need to take into account the level of control of the military -- the level of the local organisation when this organisation is established. Regarding this control, the Prosecution has offered evidence of documents signed by General Roso. This was the period when Croatia was assisting in the creation of the HVO. Then the Prosecution also says that Blaskic took over the function of the organisation which was previously established by General Bobetko. That is not true. General Bobetko had established a forward command post in Bosnia. It was placed in Central Bosnia, and it was the forward command post of the Croatian army. And Blaskic became chief of the regional staff of the HVO. Before that body was set up, there was only a forward command post of the HV army there. The Prosecution also says that the HV provided logistics support, but the Appeals Chamber in Tadic decided that the evidence on logistics support and similar support does not rise to sufficient proof. So the proof that is needed is that the Croatian army controlled the command and military operations. Next point is the military operations of the Croatian army in Bosnia. In that sense, you saw a number of orders of General Bobetko which were taken over from General Bobetko's book. Now, what are these documents all about? This is also a case of manipulating documents. To put it simply, it would be as if when the U.S. forces disembarked in Europe, let's say they committed genocide against the German people. Or let's say General Custer burnt down Indian villages, which was over a hundred years ago. Here, the conflict between the JNA and the Croatian army is portrayed as proof of international conflict, as if it was a conflict between the Croatian army and the Bosnian army. These are two different conflicts. Bobetko very clearly waged war against the JNA, and this conflict between Bobetko and the JNA cannot be equated or taken as an argument that the conflict between the BH army and the Croatian army are the same kind of war. These are different times, a different period, different participants. I have spoken about Bobetko before, and I won't go back to that, and I have also shown the map and so on. It is true that the Prosecutor is using some other arguments after the withdrawal of Bobetko and is proffering evidence on the presence of units of the Croatian army in Bosnia. It should first be noted that it emerges from all the evidence, that if the Croatian army was in Bosnia, then it was outside the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. A second point. These were not significant numbers of troops of the Croatian army, but small ones. Thirdly, in accordance with the Tadic Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber of Aleksovski, the infiltration of foreign troops in the case of a conflict between local forces does not change the character of the conflict making it from a local one in to an international one. The Defence endorses this position and wishes to underline that that position has fully denied the judgement in the Celebici case and the Rajic indictment, when the opposite position was taken, that the intervention of foreign troops changes the character of an armed conflict, transforming it from an internal in to an international one. Therefore, intervention in the submission of the Defence, and we, of course, accept the Tadic Appeals Chamber ruling and the Aleksovski ruling, that the intervention by foreign troops cannot change the character of the conflict. The Office of the Prosecutor, as evidence that Croatia cooperated with the HVO, offers a letter addressed to Tudjman asking for assistance, but that letter does not speak of control. It is true that Remi Landry of the European Monitors said that the HVO was under the control of the HV; however, he was quite explicit in saying that the European Monitoring Mission's view was not confirmed and that it was not documented. Therefore, there is no proof that the HV controlled the HVO. Can we now go into private session for a moment, please? (Private session) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Further, it should be noted that it would be quite illogical and unwise for the Republic of Croatia to advocate a change of borders. It had only just gained its independence. Yugoslavia denied the new state boundaries of the Republic of Croatia, and any raising of the issue of borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a direct threat to the sovereignty of the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, in summary, it is my submission that the Prosecution has not proven the control of the Croatian army over the HVO, and, therefore, there could not have been an international conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have expounded this in detail in our brief. But now I should like to say a few words about the status of protected persons. Namely, the indictment has to -- or, rather, the Prosecution has to prove that there was an international conflict, that the HVO was an agent of the Croatian army, but it also has to prove that Bosnian civilians had the status of protected persons in accordance with Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions. Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions says: "Persons protected by the Conventions are those who, at a given point in time and in a certain way, in the event of a conflict or occupation, should find themselves in the hands of the parties to the conflict or an occupying force whose citizens they are not." We are aware of the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision which said that control by a third state over local forces detaining civilians is far more important than citizenship of those members of the local forces, and we know that the Tadic Appeals Chamber said that in modern inter-ethnic wars, loyalty to a third state, based on ethnicity, is much more important than loyalty based on citizenship. However, with all due respect, it is our view that the decision of the Tadic Appeals Chamber is erroneous because Article IV of the Geneva Conventions explicitly and clearly requires the condition of different citizenship. The Court, in its decisions and its freedoms, has certain limits, and it is not possible to change a punitive provision at the expense of the accused. Article 2 of the Statute is a valid, legal norm. The description of the act refers to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Has the condition been fulfilled for Muslim civilians to be protected persons or not depends on whether this is a criminal act or not, and the Tribunal cannot change that. The Tribunal cannot decide retroactively to apply the law. It cannot decide to change the legal norm after the commission of a criminal act, because this is contrary to the fundamental rule of criminal law. Modern criminal penal law, at least in continental Europe, is based on the principle of legality, ever since Roman war. There is the rule, nullum crimen sine lege, which means that there is no criminal act if it did not exist in law at the time it was committed. If Article IV of the Geneva Conventions says that there must be different citizenship between the victim and the perpetrator, then the Court, after the commission of a criminal act, may not change that legal norm. That is our submission. The decision that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were, in actual fact, foreigners in relation to the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is just a test, would have very far reaching and damaging legal and political consequences. If that were so, then this Prosecutor's office should indict from Alija Izetbegovic, Halilovic, and the other generals, because the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina mobilised Croats into their own ranks, because it mobilised -- did it mobilise foreign citizens then? That is a punishable act. Similarly, Croats in Bosnia would become foreigners because all Croats were in the HVO, as all Muslims were in the BH army. So one ethnic group which is autochthonous in that state would be declared to be aliens. But even from a very ordinary, down to earth, logical standpoint, people would be declared foreigners or aliens, people who had lived together as neighbours and whose families had lived together for hundreds of years in the same villages, so then one of them would be a foreigner, another a domestic person. They would have different citizenship. Therefore, it is our position that the Bosnian Muslims cannot have the status of protected persons according to the Geneva Conventions because they had the same citizenship as Bosnian Croats. Some Bosnian Croats took Croatian citizenship, but no one renounced Bosnian citizenship. There is no evidence of that. General Blaskic is a Bosnian citizen just as he is a Croatian citizen. There is another problem which explains why Bosnian Muslims, in the hands of the HVO, cannot be considered protected persons according to the Geneva Conventions. Namely, Common Article IV of the Geneva Conventions says that: "Citizens of allied states will not be considered protected persons, as long as the state whose citizens they are maintains normal diplomatic relations with the state in whose hands they are." So one condition is the existence of a diplomatic relations and the other is the alliance. I think that these relations existed throughout, and no one called that in question. Diplomatic relations were not suspended and they functioned between Croatia and Bosnia, as did various other institutions between the two countries. The question is whether relations between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina can be called relations between allies. The Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina never declared war upon one another, which is not the case with Yugoslavia. Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia were the first to recognise each other, to establish diplomatic relations, which have never been interrupted. On the 21st of July, 1992, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia signed an agreement on friendship, and we will be coming back to that. Embassies were established in both countries, and diplomatic contacts were maintained on a regular basis. The conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO did not result in the suspension of this agreement between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, agreements in trade and all others that were in force. The conflict between the HVO and the BH army did not affect the nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia, for instance. They were not put away in any kind of centres. On the contrary, they were given assistance, and they lived like any other citizens of countries with which Croatia maintains diplomatic relations. No commercial relations were suspended, which is normal in the case of countries that are at war with one another. Throughout the time of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia was a vast, logistic base for Bosnia-Herzegovina, up to 1993. I have already said that all the military equipment passed through Croatian hands or Croatian airports. Croatia gave direct assistance to the BH army, as it did in 1992, or it allowed third parties to use Croatian territory for transiting such deliveries to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can we go into private session again, please, briefly? utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore, on the 21st of July, 1992, Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic signed an agreement, which is called an agreement on friendship and cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. As we can see, that agreement was never broken off. We have omitted Article 2. In any event, in Article 2 of that agreement, it says, "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia shall cooperate and agree amongst each other, proceeding from the respect of their separate interests and aware of the unity of interests of their countries," and then the areas of life are listed in which they will cooperate, ranging from the economy, social affairs, health, education, science, culture, et cetera. In the text you have before you, I should like to draw your attention to the first sentence. "The state delegation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina expresses their gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for having received and provided four refugees from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina beyond the capacity of the Republic of Croatia." A very important Article, point 6 of that agreement, "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This was signed by Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman. Or point 7: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will reciprocally allow their citizens to acquire dual citizenship." So on and so forth. In the next paragraph, reference is made to military cooperation in border areas and the possibility of extending that cooperation. All this was signed on the 21st of July, 1992 by the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the president of the Republic of Croatia. I think that from this summary overview, we can come to the conclusion that the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were allies, that they never broke off diplomatic relations, that they never prevented the activities of diplomatic representatives in the other state, and that for that reason, Muslim civilians in the hands of the HVO cannot enjoy the status of protected persons. Allow me now briefly to refer to the situation in the Lasva Valley. In the Aleksovski judgement, it is clearly stated, and that has been accepted by the Prosecution, and that is that an international conflict has to be proven in the time and place relevant to the indictment. The problem is when was there an international armed conflict according to the indictment? According to the indictment, it was throughout 1992 and 1993. However, the Prosecutor, in describing actual acts, mentions January 1993 and onwards. But to save time, we will skip over 1992, as we have no criminal offences, and anyway, there were no conflicts between the BH army and the HVO; there were only individual incidents, but not an armed conflict between two armies. Also in 1992, you will remember that Generals Arif Pasalic and Ante Prkacin formed a joint command of the BH army and the HVO, and that joint command was effective during the defence of Jajce and in the area of Central Bosnia. The first conflict occurred in January 1993 in Busovaca, but it only lasted two days. It did not spread to other municipalities, not even to the Lasva Valley. In Vitez, it was peaceful, and there was cooperation between the BH army and the HVO. For these reasons, and to economise with time, we will not analyse that conflict, but whatever we say about the April conflict and conflicts that followed in 1993 also apply to this conflict in January. So can I now approach the relief for a moment? When does an international or an internal armed conflict begin? In any event, the armed conflict in the Lasva Valley started on the 16th of April. Quickly, the Lasva Valley was covered by forces in this way, as you can see here. For a time, Travnik was totally cut off by the forces of the BH army, prevented the HVO to go to Herzegovina and come back. So that we can say that the HVO was fully surrounded in the Lasva enclave. In this enclave, in this specific territory and the time, that is, from 16th April, 1993 onwards, was there an international armed conflict here or not? If we apply the tests from the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision, then we will see that it simply was not an international armed conflict. One of those tests mentioned there is that the army of Republika Srpska and the JNA transferred offices between each other. In Central Bosnia, there were no HV offices. Blaskic issued orders to establish that. The return report was that there were none. Also, in the Tadic judgement, it says that salaries were paid to officers of the Republika Srpska. No one received money here from Zagreb or Mostar. The JNA was transformed into the army of the Republika Srpska. Here you saw that the army was autochthonous, consisting of local inhabitants. In the Tadic judgement, it says that the structure of ranks was the same. In the HVO, there were no ranks. Colonel Blaskic was the only person with a rank in Central Bosnia. The JNA coordinated the activities of the army of Republika Srpska. Here, the HVO was surrounded by the forces of the BH army which were seven to ten times stronger than the HVO. What did they do? They dug trenches in front of Croatian villages and defended its territory. There was no movement of forces. Even if we were to accept that Croatia's aim was a secession of part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its annexation to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO of Central Bosnia could not have had the same goal because it was surrounded by vast Muslim forces and territory inhabited by Muslim forces. That small piece of land in the heart of Bosnia could not have been annexed to Croatia. That the HVO did not have any such political aims can be seen from the activities of the HVO. Never once did the HVO try to make a breakthrough towards the south, towards Herzegovina, to link up with Herzegovina, to create a compact territory and attach to Croatia. What is also interesting is never did forces from Herzegovina try to penetrate and reach Central Bosnia so as to create the military preconditions for this territory's annexation to the Republic of Croatia. This territory did not border with the territory of the Republic of Croatia, which is also important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And aid from the Republic of Croatia finally. This territory did not receive aid from the Republic of Croatia and could not receive aid. Occasional helicopter flights, which were rare, could bring in a maximum of two tonnes of cargo, and in the Lasva Valley, this enclave needed two tonnes of flour a day to survive. You heard, General Blaskic, that they ate rice, lentils, and margarine. A box of cigarettes cost a hundred marks. All this shows is that there were no supplies, there were no supplies coming in. Never were there any Croatian army troops in the Lasva Valley. We will refer to some statements by independent observers to corroborate this submission. First, Prosecution witness, Alistair Duncan.
