utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We could cite several more witnesses. No witness ever saw any Croatian army unit in the Lasva River Valley. I would like to point one more thing that the Prosecution simply fled from, and that is the fact that the HVO and the BH army had a joint command in Central Bosnia. They had it during the time. So General Prkacin and Pasalic, in 1992, they had it. After the January conflict, you will recall that Merdan, on behalf of the 3rd Corps, and Nakic, on behalf of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and even after the conflict of the 16th of April, they had it, and they were solving civilian problems, something that the diplomatic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Nobilo. The interpreters are having difficulty in following you, and there is a lag in relation to the transcript. Please think of the interpreters but also of the Judges. So please slow down a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. I'm also chasing time at the same time, but I'm almost done. The key, when considering the issue of international conflict, is to take into account this: That the HVO and the BH army in Central Bosnia for most of the part of the relevant period had a joint command, which speaks amply about the state of allegiance, that is, of an alliance between those two parties. For all these reasons, we believe that there were no conditions for the application of Article 2 of the Statute on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially not in the small enclaves such as the Lasva River Valley, Central Bosnia. So Article 2 of this Statute cannot be applied in the case of General Blaskic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I feel like a racecar driver changing tires in the pit, Mr. President, but it's time to go. The trial is nearing an end. I have three areas I will try and address before handing the baton or the driver's seat back to Mr. Nobilo. They are detention crimes, forcible transfer, and destruction of religious objects. First, I'm compelled to say a word about General Blaskic's credibility and his testimony in this case. The issues on which the Prosecutor specifically attacked his credibility are not of particular importance to the case, but his credibility is of importance to the case. Because if you believe his testimony, then based on what he said, by definition, he did not have the mens rea sufficient to commit the crimes alleged in the indictment. Also, if you find that the asserted lies that the Prosecutor has thrown at him are not well-founded, then that tells you also something about their strategy and what they were forced to do in their closing argument. What were those asserted lies? Well, the first one I counted and culled out of my notes was the assertion that after Blaskic took over the Operative Zone command, he received orders from General Roso, and the Prosecutor asserted that they asked Blaskic what was Roso's role, and Blaskic said, "I don't know." That is asserted to have been a lie. Well, what was Blaskic actually asked and what did he really answer? If we could turn on the ELMO, please? We're going to look at page 20457. Here's what was actually said. This was cross-examination by Mr. Kehoe. "Q At the time Ante Roso was issuing these orders to you and you met him and he appointed you Lieutenant-Colonel, he was a General in the HV, wasn't he? A First of all, as far as issuing orders to me, that's what you said. I didn't say this before this Court. He issued orders to the commander of the municipal staff of the HVO in Kiseljak." Now for what matters. "A Second, as far as I know, he was an officer of the main staff of the HVO, I say, as far as I know. General Ante Roso did not take out his order of appointment and say, 'Well, that is the order and I am so and so.' He did not take out a document of that kind and show me that, and I assume that he was an officer of the main staff of the HVO." That's the end of the answer to that question. That's what General Blaskic told you. He told you exactly what the nature of the encounter was, that nothing specific was discussed on the subject, and he assumed that Roso was acting on the main staff of the HVO. You can decide whether the Prosecution has demonstrated that our client lied or whether they're spinning these things out of whole cloth to try and impugn his credibility and turn you, in some way, to view him as a dishonest, irreputable person. Alleged lie number 2 was asserted to be Blaskic's testimony that the troops stopped at the barricade in Ahmici on the 20th of October, 1992 were going to Jajce and not to Novi Travnik. The proof of this supposed lie was said to be a news report, Prosecution Exhibit 646. If we could put that on the ELMO, please. What is P646? This is a transcript of home video footage apparently shot on the night of April 16th, 1993 by someone, and it appears to have later been played on TV Busovaca, which someone else taped, and then they gave it to the Prosecutor, and this is a transcript. Let's look at the transcript, and you'll see the portion I've highlighted. The statement that is relevant is attributed to journalist, and it reads: "Ahmici, the first and last stronghold of the Muslim armed forces. The point where they tried to stop members of the Croatian Defence Council who were on their way to positions in Novi Travnik." That is the basis of the supposed lie by General Blaskic, that it is his belief that the HVO forces that were stopped at the roadblock were going to Jajce, not to Novi Travnik. Who is this journalist? It's an unknown, anonymous person. Are they making this statement based on some observation in October of 1992? We don't know. This was filmed on 16 April, 1993. Why were they making this report? Were they making it to inflame the Croat population in Busovaca? Is this more propaganda? We don't know. We don't even know who the speaker is. You're in a position to determine whether this demonstrates that General Blaskic is a liar or whether something else is true with respect to the Prosecutor's arguments. Alleged lie number three is the claim that Blaskic never, in his direct testimony, told the Court he was ever in Novi Travnik in relation to the October 1992 conflict there. What is the evidence in that regard? The evidence is Stewart, Colonel Stewart, went to Novi Travnik on the 20th of October and told you that Blaskic was not there. Did Blaskic never tell you whether he was in Novi Travnik or, rather, did he never tell you that he was in Novi Travnik in October of 1992? If we could put the next transcript portion on the ELMO, page 21385. Here's the question and here's the answer: "Q General, when you met in Novi Travnik on the 21st, what did you talk about, you and Kordic? A I informed them on what agreement we had reached with Merdan and what I had expected of the TO and what else we should do in order to stabilise this cease-fire." He told you he was in Novi Travnik on the 21st of October. Why did the Prosecutor say he never did? Why are they so desperate to convince you that he's a liar? He further explained in his testimony, General Blaskic, that is, that he was not in Novi Travnik on 20 October because he was cut off by the barricade in Ahmici. He had been in Mostar trying to get aid to fight against the Serbs in Jajce, because at the time the situation in Jajce was quite desperate. They also assert that Prosecutor's Exhibit 647 establishes that Blaskic was actually in Novi Travnik on the 20th of October, but if you look at that document, that is a document saying that "Kordic and I are in Novi Travnik commanding the HVO," but the time and date of the document are now displayed on the ELMO. That document is from the 21st of October, 21.00, which is when Blaskic told you he was in Novi Travnik. If we put the third page of the report on the ELMO, please, you'll see that it speaks of the present, not of the past. It says: "Kordic and I are in Novi Travnik." It doesn't say "yesterday," it says today, the 21st of October, 1992, which is what he told you in his testimony. Now I need to turn to detention crimes. First I will speak of detention crimes per se and then I will turn to the issue of forced labour. First, it is important to understand exactly what the charge is in the indictment in this regard, and that is because detention of civilians in wartime is not alleged to be a crime, nor is it a crime per se. Rather, the crimes alleged in this indictment are that detainees were held in inhumane conditions or were forced to dig trenches or were used as hostages or were used as human shields. The framing of these charges is in apparent recognition that civilians may be detained for security reasons, such as the existence of combat operations in the area. And, indeed, it was not illegal to detain military-age men in the Lasva Valley, nor in areas adjacent to the Lasva Valley on the other side of the front line, that is, by the BH forces, because as the ICRC commentary to Article 42 to the Geneva Convention IV states at page 258, that although the fact that men are of military age is not a per se basis for detention, that is not the case if there is "a danger of him being able to join the enemy armed force." In other words, if there are men of military age of the opposing force who -- or of the opposing group who can transit and are able to join the enemy armed forces, those persons may be detained. I simply provide this background to make perfectly clear why detention per se is not illegal and it is not charged here as a crime. The issue here is whether Blaskic ordered or knew or had reason to know that detainees were held in inhumane conditions or were held as hostages or were used as human shields. With respect to all detainees, the evidence is uniform. Blaskic never ordered any detainees -- never ordered any civilians to be detained. What happened in the Lasva Valley? When conflict broke out on the 16th of April, military-aged men, and some women and children were detained in Vitez, Stari Vitez, Zenica, Poculica, and Kruscica. Of course, in Stari Vitez, Zenica, Poculica, and Kruscica, it was Croats who were detained, while in Vitez, it was Muslims who were detained. You've heard about in Zenica, there were three different prisons, two of which the ICRC was denied access, including the infamous music school. My point there is not to blame anyone but just to illustrate for you how this occurred. It occurred on the morning of the 16th. It occurred in the entire area. It occurred on both sides of the front line. There is no evidence in the case as to who may have ordered this activity, if, indeed, anyone ordered it. General Blaskic has testified, and the documentary evidence indicates, he did not order any detention of civilians. What happened when civilians started to be detained? This created a very negative atmosphere. Rumours circulated on both sides of the confrontation line that people were being detained. It is quite likely and normal that the process spawned further fear and gained momentum. What situation did that confront General Blaskic with? He was faced with a problem, not of his own making, a complex problem, one that had to be dealt with within a context of widespread violence and fighting and in partnership with the International Red Cross and other international agencies. What did he do when he learned there were detainees? He ordered that they be protected and adequately cared for and that they be released under the supervision of the Red Cross, and he, in fact, repeated General Petkovic's order to that effect on the 18th of April. There's no evidence that he learned of any detainees prior to the 18th of April. You'll see in point 2 of this order, he ordered the exchange of detained soldiers and civilians at once. On the 21st of April, he issued another order to ensure the proper treatment of detainees and cooperation with the Red Cross in all matters pertaining to detainees. Again, he knew that any detainees had to be treated properly, but he was looking to the Red Cross for guidance. He had never been in this situation before. He repeated this order to protect civilians and treat detainees humanely on the 24th of April, as the Court can see in this order. So we have three orders by the 24th of April ordering proper treatment and release and exchange of detainees, and he repeated this order again on the 27th of April, 1993, specifically prohibiting any treatment of detained persons contrary to the Geneva Conventions. Two days later, on the 29th of April, he again ordered the release of all detainees and also ordered, which undoubtedly was pursuant to the Red Cross procedures and requests in point 1, immediately draft lists of detained civilians, men, women, and children, including the following information, deadline 30 April. Why all the procedures? Why all the bureaucracy with respect to releasing civilians? The Prosecution chides this notion and says, "Of course, he should have just released him. How can he say that Red Cross protocols were important?" What if, Your Honours, the HVO had simply gone into the cinema and said, "Okay, who wants to go to Zenica, raise your hand?" And 30 people raised their hand. They put them in a truck, they take them to the checkpoint, and they go across the checkpoint. What would happen then? Whoever did that would be here on trial for ethnic cleansing, for forcible transfer. The reason the Red Cross insists on lists and interviews is to ensure that people can voluntarily, without any coercion, pressure, or intimidation, can voluntarily decide where to go, to stay on one side of the front line or go on the other. Indeed, when there are persons who did put people in a truck and take them to the checkpoint, those situations are being referred to as a war crime in this Court. That's the Prosecutor's definition of forcible transfer. So it's easy to say, to belittle the adherence to ICRC protocols, but I've explained our views on that. I'll proceed. In this order of 29 April, General Blaskic specifically ordered that safety be guaranteed for these released civilians. Why was that important? That was important so that civilians could truly and freely decide where they wanted to go, and so they wouldn't be forced or intimidated into leaving the area, which will be something I address when I talk about forcible transfer in a moment. Your Honour, when would you like to take the break this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was waiting for you to ask for it for a change, Mr. Hayman. Yes. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. We've all had a break. Please be seated. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, during the rather long break, I think you had time not only to change the wheels but also the engine, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We are raring to go. I was saying that between the 18th and 29th of April, we just reviewed, there were five orders from Colonel Blaskic directed to proper treatment and release of detainees. We ask that you consider those five orders in conjunction with the evidence on command and control and what actual ability he had to force people to take action with respect to detainees, particularly considering who held the detainees, the Vitezovi and, for the most part, the military police. In addition, at times, there was local and civilian resistance to the release of detainees. Blaskic continued to press for their release, both directly and through the work of the joint commission, but when civilian authorities disagreed with him, they would act how they wished to act and not comply with his request. For example, this testimony was received from EC monitor Morsink. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Let me ask you, on the 3rd of May, did Skopljak and Santic, would you say it would be fair to describe what occurred at that meeting is as follows: 'They were a pair of hard-liners, and they did not want to release prisoners. They said that they had received orders to release the prisoners, but they refused to do so.' Is that accurate? A That's accurate ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In any event, I've been talking about the mere fact of detention, but since it's not detention but rather inhumane treatment that is alleged, I will return to the latter. Did Blaskic know or have reason to know of any inhumane conditions under which detainees may have been held, and did he fail to act? If you look at the five orders I've just summarised, most or all of them indicate that proper treatment should be provided to detainees. There is also evidence, Your Honours, that detainees in Vitez were generally held in good conditions. In the Vitez cinema, for example, according to both witness testimony and Prosecutor's Exhibit 529, the EC monitor's report, detainees were treated well. During the day, they were allowed to go home to eat, shower, or obtain a change of clothing, and persons were allowed to bring food to the cinema. Only military-aged men were detained at the cinema. I'm paraphrasing directly from that EC monitor's report. Hostage taking. Were any detainees held as hostages? Did Blaskic ever order the taking of civilians as hostages for the purpose of exchange? There is no evidence that he did, and there are many orders, not only directing proper treatment for civilians and detainees, but also telling HVO units not to arrest civilians. What does that mean? That's an order not to detain a civilian, including not to detain them for the purpose of having chips to barter in any future exchange situation. I've already recounted some of those orders, but here's one in which he expressly said to HVO units, this is June 19, point 1, "stop the arresting of civilians." He made that very clearly. Now, were detainees at the cinema held as hostages? Was there an intent to hold them as hostages? I've already said that, according to the EC monitors, only military-aged men were held there. We point out that there had been a general mobilisation, both on the HVO and the BH army side, throughout the territory of all military-aged men, and that occurred prior to the 16th of April. That informs Your Honours on the question of whether military-aged men were detained at the cinema for purposes of security concerns or were they taken with the intent of being held as hostages? There was one incident of threatened hostage taking which is very instructive in that it should inform the Court of Blaskic's attitude towards such misconduct and the action he took. We need to go into private session for just a moment while I describe it. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were any detainees used as human shields, and if so, does General Blaskic have direct or command responsibility for any such misconduct? The Prosecution has alleged three instances of human shield use, Merdani in January or February of 1993, Vitez on 16 April, and Vitez on 20 April. In Merdani, there was testimony from several individuals that detainees were used as human shields in and around Merdani. This was in Busovaca in late January 1993 when then Colonel Blaskic was in Kiseljak. There's no evidence that the incident was ever raised with him or that he ever got a report about it. In Vitez, on the 16th of April, Dr. Mujezinovic testified at a meeting in the cinema complex that Santic and Skopljak threatened to kill Muslim detainees if the BH army continued to advance. That was actually on the 19th, although the indictment charges the incident on the 16th. Blaskic didn't order this threat. He didn't know about it. He didn't learn about it thereafter. Moreover, there's an interesting legal question as to this threat. The threat was never made to the detainees. It was said to Dr. Mujezinovic, and Dr. Mujezinovic was asked to call the BH army. But the detainees were never told, "You are a human shield. You are being used for this purpose." The violation of using human shields is if the human shield constitutes inhuman, cruel, or inhumane treatment to the detainee, and if no violence is ever perpetrated on the detainee and they are never told, never subjected to any intimidation, any threat, they don't even know about these statements being made that were removed from them, there is a legal question as to whether that constitutes inhuman, cruel, or inhumane treatment. But as I said, this conduct was not directed or condoned in any way by Colonel Blaskic. Vitez, the 20th of April. A single witness, who I believe testified in open session, Advija Hrustic, testified that Bosnian Muslims from Gacice were taken to the front of the Hotel Vitez on the 20th of April. Her testimony was that one soldier said to her, "You're going to sit here now and let your people shell you because they have been shelling us up to now, and you better sit down and wait." That was one soldier, one HVO soldier, according to the witness, said this to her. A few hours later, the villagers returned to Gacice unharmed. If the unidentified soldier, in fact, made this taunting statement to Ms. Hrustic, we do not condone it and then Colonel Blaskic never condoned it, but at the same time, that statement if made, we submit, does not, under the circumstances present, constitute the crime of the use of a human shield. There's no evidence, apart from that one alleged hearsay statement, of any intent on anyone's part to place these villagers in front of the hotel in order to shield the building from indirect fire. In fact, the witness's testimony suggests the opposite, namely, that the villagers were temporarily removed from Gacice during what was combat activity occurring on that day and were returned after the combat had concluded. In other words, they were removed from the area for security and legitimate security reasons. There's also no evidence that the Hotel Vitez was shelled at or before this time period on the 20th of April. According to Hrustic, no shells fell in the immediate area at the time. That's in the reporter's transcript at 4849. This suggests that what occurred was although regrettable and inappropriate, it was the mere taunting by one soldier of one individual. In any event, there's no evidence that Colonel Blaskic ordered, knew, or had reason to know of this taunt. Ms. Hrustic was not able to provide a time period in her testimony as to when this happened, when they were outside the hotel, and there is no evidence that Colonel Blaskic observed the villagers in the area of the hotel. The Prosecution chose not to present any other witnesses, such as a second villager, there were apparently a large number of them, presumably because no one else heard the alleged taunt and no one else was aware of any shelling that might have occurred earlier in the day in Vitez. There's been a suggestion by the Prosecution that the housing of detainees in the cinema, which was adjacent to the Workers' University building, was illegal. The testimony has been that the cinema was a well-built structure that was safer for housing detainees than any other structure in Vitez. The ECMM noted in a report that the housing of detainees there might be a technical or formal violation of the Geneva Convention. This is an enlargement of one of the Prosecutor's Exhibits, 45H, and it depicts the Workers' University building and the cinema. The vertical building, the building that's a little bit wider but not as long, is the cinema building. The "T," at the top of the "T" is the Workers' University building. The question under applicable law apparently, at least in part, is whether this is one building or two. In fact, the persons detained in the cinema, were they housed in the same building as the Vitez brigade, which apparently occupied some or all of the Workers' University, or are these two buildings? If you look at these photographs, Your Honours, I think you can reasonably conclude that although these buildings are adjacent and they may have a hallway or passageway between them, they appear to be, in significant respects, two structures. We think, under the circumstances, it would be wrong to hold General Blaskic criminally accountable for something that might hinge on whether this hallway between these two buildings constitutes a hallway or a connection such that it's only one building, considering the fact, Your Honours, that at the time, no one came to him and suggested that there was a safer location for these detainees, pending interviews, lists, and release. No one has testified in this case that any suggestion was made to him that these persons should be moved. Would it be fair to impose a custodial sentence on him for this act, under those circumstances? We submit it would not be. Forced labour. The war in Central Bosnia consisted largely of trench warfare reminiscent of World War I. The use of forced labour to dig trenches in Central Bosnia occurred on both sides of the conflict. One reason is that you can order a soldier to dig his own foxhole or trench, but if a soldier can find another person to dig it for him, he may well try. To accomplish these fortifications, both the BH authorities and the Herceg-Bosna civil authorities mobilised citizens in an area they controlled into work platoons or working platoons. Now, what is the charge in the indictment with respect to forced labour? The forced labour charge appeared in the persecution count, Count 1, and in Counts 13 and 14, which provide or allude to inhumane or cruel treatment of detainees. In both of these locations, Count 1 and Count 13/14, the exclusive charge is that detainees were forced to dig trenches. No where is it charged that non-detainees or members of working platoons were forced to dig trenches. That is because the use of working platoons per se is not illegal. It is not illegal to mobilise citizens into working platoons and force them to engage in labour, including the digging of fortifications, so long as the conditions are not dangerous or abusive, nor is the practice imposed in a discriminatory manner. Now, we have prepared a chart to try and illustrate for the Court, and I have copies I'd like to hand out with the help of the registrar, but in the meantime, and this is a series I'll be getting to, but the first one for the moment is on the video monitor, and I think I should go ahead in order to use the time. What does this chart illustrate? It illustrates the state of current international humanitarian law on the use of detainees versus work platoons to prepare fortifications. At the left margin, a distinction is made between detainees at the top and work platoons or non-detainees at the bottom. The two categories across the top of the chart are, on the left, the existence of an international armed conflict and, on the right, the existence of an internal armed conflict. Inside each box, we have indicated whether the particular activity is charged as a crime in the indictment and whether or not the particular activity is a violation of international humanitarian law. If you look first at the bottom two boxes, working platoons or non-detainees, you will see that in both international and internal armed conflict, the use of working platoons or non-detainees for fortifying the terrain are not charged as a crime, and, indeed, you will find that it's not a violation of humanitarian law in either circumstance. If you look in the top two boxes, you will see that both, and that relates to the use of detainees for forced labour, you will find that both of those conditions or, rather, situations are charged in the indictment as crimes, but you'll find that in an internal armed conflict, we submit that forced labour of civilian detainees is not illegal in an internal armed conflict. We hope this provides a useful framework for analysing the evidence in this case because it is quite interesting how the evidence has been presented with respect to this charge. Before we get to the evidence, we'll use this chart, in part, to illustrate for the Court that working platoons, which is the bottom two boxes, were part of the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna and that they were legal under all international humanitarian laws. This is significant because we believe it resulted in -- this issue resulted in a certain amount of miscommunication between international observers and the joint commission, when there were joint commission meetings, and, indeed, this misunderstanding has spilled over to this very courtroom. Let me give you one example. The UNHCR protested to the joint commission that Gypsies in Vitez were being taken to dig trenches. This is Mr. Morsink. (Videotape played) "A The International Red Cross and the UNHCR were present at those types of meetings, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: (redacted)"

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So that's an example of UNHCR protesting to the joint commission that Gypsies in Vitez were being forced to dig trenches. Well, what do we know about those Gypsies? 1) They were never detained. There's no charge, there's no evidence that Gypsies in Vitez were ever detained. So this protest to the joint commission did not involve detainees. 2) We know from the documents that the Prosecutor introduced in his rebuttal case, P715 to P717, that these Gypsies were in working platoons from the Sofa and Zic districts outside of Vitez, and we'll look at those documents in a moment. This distinction between detainees and non-detainees was not made by the Prosecution in the presentation of their case. They regularly questioned witnesses about the use of civilians without specifying whether they were talking about detainees or not. Listen to this exchange, please, between the Prosecutor and Mr. Morsink. (Videotape played) "Mr. Harmon: Q I'd like to turn to another topic and that would be the subject of the use of civilians to perform forced labour, specifically trench-digging. While you were in Central Bosnia, were you aware of this particular practice? A I was given protests according to -- which said that civilians had been forced to dig trenches. I was given this during the meeting of the joint commission. During the meeting, I was made aware of 15 protests in that respect, more, 10 to 15, 10 to 15."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What does this tell Your Honours? Here we have the testimony of EC monitor Morsink being asked by the Prosecution, "Was the use of civilians to dig trenches protested to the joint commission?" Answer: "Yes, 10 to 15 times." Civilians, not civilian detainees. You didn't hear the word "detainees" anywhere in the question or the answer. That's not what was being discussed. They were discussing civilians. Given that you know there were working platoons in the area, that is what is being discussed, and that's also the case you just saw with respect to the example of Gypsies outside Vitez and UNHCR raising it with the joint commission. They weren't talking about detainees. Detainees being forced to perform labour is the only charge in this indictment pertaining to forced labour. There is no charge that civilians being forced to perform labour is illegal or that it occurred or that General Blaskic has any responsibility for any such conduct, even if it were illegal. Consequently, with very few exceptions, the record in this case pertains to the use of civilian labour to dig fortifications, not the use of detainees. What about the working platoons? To be lawful, working platoon duties must be imposed in a non-discriminatory manner and must not involve dangerous work at the front lines. Now, as I've said, the use of non-detained civilians to perform labour isn't charged in the indictment and should not be considered by you in your deliberations, but we maintain nonetheless that the practice, at least insofar as Colonel Blaskic was aware of it, and he was aware of the use of working platoons, it was legal. He thought it was legal, and what he understood to be occurring was legal, because the work platoons in Vitez generally met these requirements. You may recall the testimony of Dusan Lukovic. He is a Serb resident of Vitez. In fact, he was the former president of the municipality of Vitez. He was in a working platoon in Vitez, and he testified that every village had its own platoon, that work duty was imposed on all men under the age of 60. There were Serbs, Gypsies, Croats, and Muslims in the working platoons. There was no discrimination based on nationality. All work platoon members received credit towards their pensions for the same amount of years of service, as if they had served in an HVO combat unit. Mr. Lukovic also testified that conditions for the working platoons were not dangerous, were not abusive. They received three meals a day. They were not worked beyond endurance. They slept. They had an evening break to sleep if the work lasted more than one day, and that the HVO soldiers would routinely secure the work area, protect them, and if danger started to arise, the work duties would cease, and the members of the work platoons would move out of any area of danger. Colonel Blaskic never ordered or acquiesced in any dangerous, discriminatory, or abusive conditions for work platoons. Again, in their final brief, the Prosecutor makes no distinction between detainees being forced to perform labour and working platoons or non-detainees engaging in fortification of the land. This is a fatal defect in the Prosecutor's presentation in this area. At the end of his case, the Prosecutor introduced certain documents relating to work platoons in the Vitez area. What do those documents show? Work platoons were established by the civilian authorities under applicable laws and regulations. They were multi-ethnic. This is what their own documents, P715 to 717, show. Work platoons did not consist of detainees but rather ordinary citizens, and, in fact, we would suggest that they were not civilians within the meaning of that phrase as used in the indictment because they were mobilised into the working platoons. They received a pension based on the work they performed. The Prosecution argues that an order in September of 1993, in which Colonel Blaskic asked for work platoon support in the Grbavica area after the front line had moved beyond Grbavica, that that is somehow illegal. That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 715. Page 3 of that document does reflect that there was a request by Blaskic for assistance from work platoons in the Grbavica area after the battle was over on the 8th of September and after the front line had moved forward past and off the Grbavica feature. The Prosecution made no attempt to prove that the front line was not pushed off of the Grbavica feature, and the record does not reflect that this assignment requested by Colonel Blaskic in P715 was in any way dangerous, exposed the work platoon members to any enemy fire, or that it resulted in any injuries. Now, it does reflect regrettably, on page 3, that there was some disturbance in the course of the performance of this work in or around Grbavica and some member or members of the working platoon were beaten by an HVO soldier. It's for unknown reasons. We're not told in the report. There is no indication of the nationality of the victims of this beating, and there's been no other evidence presented. We don't know if they were Muslim or Croat or Serb or Gypsy. In any event, this conduct, whatever it is, it is not charged because these are not detainees, these are working platoons, and that's true of the activity in all of these documents. You can review them and, we think, reach that same conclusion. As opposed to the work of working platoons, Colonel Blaskic knew that forced labour by detainees was illegal and he took measures to prevent such conduct. What did he do? In 1992, he had Red Cross information cards distributed to all HVO soldiers indicating, in clear and simple words and pictures, that civilians had to be protected, sheltered, and not be abused in any way. That was in 1992 that he had these calendars distributed and again in 1993. The one you're looking at is the 1993 to 1994 version. The Prosecution argues that Blaskic must have known, must have seen detainees digging trenches, and so he's guilty. First of all, Your Honours, since fortification by work platoon members is legal, and yet the same conduct by detainees is illegal, how are you supposed to tell? If you're driving by on the roadside and you see somebody digging and you see a soldier with them, is that soldier guarding detainees or is he protecting them and looking out for the detainees? It's almost impossible to tell, if simply driving by. But furthermore, their own evidence belies the fact that this is some kind of a practice that would be easily observed. What did the humanitarian affairs officer from BritBat, Lee Whitworth, testify concerning this fact? (Videotape played) "Judge Riad: The fact of how these trenches are being built and by whom, by the -- would it also be the duty of the detainees or would it be the commanders? A The actual digging of the trenches would have been the local militia on the ground. I saw no evidence of civilians or prisoners digging trenches."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's Lee Whitworth, the humanitarian affairs officer for the British Battalion who served in Bosnia from May 1993 until November of 1993. When Blaskic was alerted to the allegation of forced labour of Bosnian Muslim civilian detainees, he took actions to stop it and he made it perfectly clear within the HVO that the use of detainees for forced labour was strictly forbidden, and we've prepared for you, Your Honours, a summary chart of some, not all, but some of the orders designed to inform and enforce among HVO soldiers and units humanitarian laws, including the protection of civilians and the prohibition of the treatment of any detained civilians contrary to the Geneva Convention, including the digging of trenches. I'm not going to read them all. These particular orders on this chart pertain to observance of the laws of war. As you can see, there are a number of orders. We submit that it cannot be said, for all these reasons, that Colonel Blaskic failed to take reasonable measures to ensure, to the best of his ability, that adequate conditions and treatment of detainees and that their speedy release be achieved. I'd like to address one more item before asking Mr. Nobilo to make a few closing remarks, and that is forcible transfer. This is alleged in Count 1, and it is alleged therein that General Blaskic has liability for the forcible transfer of civilians. The Prosecutor alleges that the HVO forcibly transferred Bosnian Muslim civilians by terror, by detention and expulsion, and by exchange of detainees. There is no question that there were large population movements in Central Bosnia in 1993. These movements began in 1992 when a tremendous influx of refugees, particularly Bosnian Muslim refugees, into Central Bosnia occurred after they had been expelled from areas controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. Muslim refugees thus came into these areas in large numbers in 1992, which is contrary to the charges in the indictment. To explain why these movements occurred, the Prosecutor called Mr. Kajmovic. He was a former SDA politician in Vitez who testified about certain statistics he had attempted to gather on population movements. He didn't offer any scientific conclusions about the reasons for those movements, but he did offer conclusions as to why persons moved, based on his political beliefs. I just would like to remind Your Honours of an observation that one of you made at the time he testified, and that is you, Judge Jorda. (Videotape played) "Judge Jorda: ... political questions, you could answer with mathematics, and if you were being asked about statistics for which it didn't have the facts, you defended yourself with your convictions. That is your political thesis."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Why did people move? We know that in Ahmici, people were driven from their homes or murdered. But what about elsewhere? Some moved out of a concern that fighting might come to their locale. Some moved because fighting broke out in or near their village. Some moved because their village came under the control of the other party to the conflict and they wished to reside in territory controlled by their own army. For example, that occurred in Gacice with the help of international agencies, according to the Prosecutor's witness, Mr. Kajmovic. (Videotape played) "Mr. Nobilo: Q In these interviews, Mr. Kajmovic, did you come across, for instance, the cases that, for instance, from Gacice, the population left under the protection of the international forces? A Yes. I have certain data reflecting that for Gacice."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I note, as an aside, the Prosecutor submitted no percipient witness testimony as to how those Gacice villagers actually left Gacice. They did leave. There's testimony that they asked to leave some days before they left. But no percipient witness has testified as to how they left and who moved them. The only evidence you have is their own demographer, Mr. Kajmovic, that they left with the assistance of international agencies. The Defence finds that curious, that there's no percipient witness, only hearsay evidence offered on that point. In any event, why else did people move? Fighting-aged men who were detained frequently asked to be allowed to leave for Zenica or Travnik because they wanted to rejoin their BH army unit. The families of such men then typically asked to be moved or exchanged or allowed to leave so that they could reunite their family. These movements tended to be symmetrical: Muslims moved in one direction; Croats moved in another. If we can go into private session for a moment, I'd like to present what is perhaps the most articulate explanation of why people moved that this Court heard from a court witness. (Private session) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted) 21 (redacted) 22 (redacted) 23 (redacted) 24 (redacted) 25 (redacted) 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted) 12 (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: All of these movements occurred in whole or in part with the help of or under the supervision of various agencies, the Red Cross, UNPROFOR, UNHCR. We're not suggesting that was wrong. It was unfortunate that these fears and conditions caused these population movements, but it was not a crime to let people move when they insisted on moving. It was not a crime when international humanitarian organisations facilitated this, and it was not a crime even if Colonel Blaskic allowed people to cross the front line in order to move to another region. The Prosecution has not proven a single instance in which Blaskic ordered, acquiesced, or failed to act to counter activity designed to drive Bosnian Muslim civilians from their homes through violence or intimidation. On the contrary, he worked diligently to forbid and punish acts when they occurred by HVO soldiers that did intimidate Muslim citizens and cause them to want to leave HVO-controlled areas. There are many, many, many orders he issued to provide to try and improve security for the population, to try and prevent acts of violence against Muslim civilians, to stop burning of homes, to stop soldiers from occupying empty homes, to prevent the destruction of property, to forbid evictions, and so forth. I haven't counted all those orders. You have the slides. You can look at them. You can judge. Was Colonel Blaskic papering the file or was he trying to do the best he could under what were very difficult conditions fuelled by the kinds of fears that you had so eloquently described a moment ago in closed session. Was it within Colonel Blaskic's power to create an environment of complete security for Muslim citizens resident within the Vitez enclave? Part of the problem was there was no part, if you look at the relief map, you can see that there was no part of the enclave that was more than 1.000 metres away from the front line. Wherever you went, even at the very centre, you were within about a thousand metres from the front line, which is still a danger zone. It was all a war zone. The whole Vitez enclave was a war zone, and the testimony in this case has been anyone who could leave did leave, because who would want to live in such a place during such a war? I want to briefly discuss, just in five minutes, count 14, destruction of religious or educational objects. In Duhri, there's been no showing, that's the incident in August 1992, where there was a roadblock in Duhri within 100 metres of the mosque. There has been no evidence of any significant damage to the mosque. There's a pock mark on the mosque. No one ever raised a complaint or a cry about it. In Ahmici, we know what destroyed those mosques, and we don't condone those attacks, but neither did Colonel Blaskic. In Stari Vitez, the claim is that the roof of the mosque was destroyed or damaged -- excuse me, by the truck bomb. We've talked about the truck bomb. In the Vitez enclave, that's it. There are no other Muslim religious or educational institutions that are alleged to have been destroyed. That is it. Now, there are others, particularly in the Kiseljak enclave, but we ask you to do the following in determining Colonel Blaskic's responsibility for destruction to Muslim religious or educational institutions: What did he do about the problem, particularly of vandalisation to such objectives by unknown persons? He issued specific orders, such as point 2 of this order, forbidding such actions by HVO soldiers, and when he learned of incidents, he acted, this is an order on the 17th of August with respect to a religious building in Kiseljak that he heard through the grapevine, he didn't get a report of this damage or destruction, he testified, but he heard through unofficial channels, I believe, that the mosque had been damaged, and he sent this sternly-worded order to Ivica Rajic to try and get an investigation going. The other thing we ask you to do in judging him on this question is the following: Ask yourselves and look at the evidence with respect to whether those Muslim religious or other cultural institutions that were outside of HVO territory but were within, say, artillery range of HVO territory, what happened to those? And why is that important, because the Prosecutor's expert, Colin Kaiser, Dr. Kaiser testified that there were many acts of vandalism by unknown perpetrators. If you look at those cultural objects that are outside of the front line, you know that Croatian vandals didn't get to those institutions, so you know you're eliminating vandalism from the picture, but still the HVO military could have shelled, could have mortared, could have destroyed all of those objects. If there was a policy to eradicate Muslims and eradicate Muslim cultural institutions from this land, the HVO could have done it and they would have done it, and General Blaskic would have directed it. But did he? I asked the question of Dr. Kaiser, the Prosecution expert, and here was his response. (Videotape played) "A One first remark is that as you remember from the first two maps, very, very little damage was done from HVO positions against mosques that were in the Armija-controlled territory. There was extremely light damage. I don't know why. I don't know if it's a question of ordinance. I don't know whether it is a question of will."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Extremely light damage to Muslim cultural objects that were not exposed to vandalism but which could have been totally destroyed by HVO military ordinance. Before I ask Mr. Nobilo to make a few concluding remarks, I want to thank the Court again, thank counsel, thank the interpreters. Mr. Nobilo and I will soon be departing The Hague. It's been a privilege to appear before Your Honours, and our client has asked us to tell you that he believes he made the right decision to voluntarily come here three years ago. He has spent three years in gaol, but he thanks you for your patience and he thanks you for the wisdom and the intellectual rigor that he knows you will bring to your verdict. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have really come to the end of these proceedings and to the end of our presentation of our final arguments. During this lengthy process, I think you often must have wondered whether the person who is in front of you, who has been sitting here, who answered your questions, was capable of committing the crimes with which he has been charged. He has spent two years here, and through several months, he answered your questions, and as experienced trial Judges, you may have been able to reach your own conclusions and certain impressions about him. Some 150 witnesses paraded in front of you. I think we have entered about 1.300 exhibits into the transcript. The witnesses came from the wartorn areas where the passions had been whipped up. They were members of the army which was opposed to General Blaskic. These were witnesses who came from a wartime atmosphere. But it is very significant that no one, not a single witness said nothing bad about General Blaskic on a personal level. I think that this is an extraordinary situation. What does this mean? What we had in Bosnia was not only a breakdown of the state institutions, but its social system, but in this inter-ethnic terrible war, the social fuses broke, and some people believed that anything was permissible. Things that were prohibited all of a sudden became permissible in the minds of many. So in an atmosphere like this, let us see how General Blaskic treated the norms of a civilised society. Let's see. The first test of his behaviour is his attitude towards property, property that was not his own. The Bible says "Steal not." While many during this war amassed wealth, General Blaskic came to Vitez carrying one soldier's suitcase, and this is how he left. While they were giving away apartments of the former JNA officers, he refused to take one. Blaskic lived in his office behind a screen and slept on a cot. That is all he had. When he learned that he had been indicted before this Trial Chamber, he packed his modest suitcase and he came over here. He received this indictment in a garage, because that is where he lived. This is one of the tests where we can see whether these fuses of social behaviour had let him down or not. General Blaskic has been accused of being part of a master plan to ethnically cleanse Muslims from a certain area through killing and burning and terror, drive them from this area. I will show you one example. This is a letter of apology which General Blaskic sent on 31 January, 1993 addressed to Mr. Mustafa Agic, who happens to be a Muslim. General Blaskic is commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Mr. Mustafa Agic is a small man who owns one inn which is his livelihood. What does he say? This is an apology for the brutal behaviour of an extremist member of the HVO. This is what General Blaskic says: "Dear sir, I have been informed by the competent authorities about the destructive behaviour of an uncontrolled group of HVO soldiers who demolished your catering establishment on 29 January, 1993." General Blaskic says that "Such acts of the extremists within the HVO are undermining the security situation and create insecurity," but he then ads that "I can promise you that appropriate measures will be taken against the perpetrators of these acts." Then he tells this small man, and this is not an event that got the attention of CNN, because our learned colleague across say that only when CNN was around they would do something, so General Blaskic says to this man, "I wish to apologise to you once again for everything that was done by the extremists in the ranks of the HVO. Sincerely, General Tihomir Blaskic." Your Honours, do you think that this letter, it testifies to General Blaskic being part of some master plan, that he's a racist, that he persecutes these Muslims? He apologises. He apologises to this citizen because the HVO caused damage to his property. This citizen happens to be a Muslim, and this is why we used it here. But, first of all, he expresses his apology to him as a citizen of the town. This is an example of his behaviour during these turbulent times. Let me paraphrase what the Prosecutor said. Blaskic left in his wake death and destruction in order to create a single ethnic state. Not only was he part of the programme of persecution, he advocated it, and this plan involved the removal of Muslims from this area. When the Prosecutor said that the other day, I asked myself, does he really believe this? I asked myself, can anybody in the Lasva Valley believe this? What do we know about what was going on in the Lasva Valley? We were not there. You were not there. I was not there in 1993. I did not live far away, but to be honest, I did not even know what was going on. What we learned about it, we learned through the witnesses and through the documents which were presented to you here. What did these witnesses say? What did the Prosecution witnesses say, those same witnesses which were called by the Prosecution to support their case? I will give you several samples of that. What does Fuad Zeco, an honourable man from Vitez, a veterinarian, and what does he say in this trial about General Blaskic? (Videotape played) "Mr. Nobilo: Q Can you just say "Yes" or "No"? Did Tihomir Blaskic ever speak against the Muslims as a people? A No."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Another statement from the same witness. (Videotape played) "Mr. Nobilo: Q What is your assessment of that appearance of Tihomir Blaskic on television? A A person who tried to resolve common problems in terms of the defence of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Ethnic tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time had peaked. An ethnic war had broken out. What did the Prosecution witness Roy Hunter tell the Court? (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Mr. Valenta expressed views which could be described as being in favour of ethnic division; correct? A Yes. Yes. Q Did you ever hear or hear of Tihomir Blaskic expressing any such views? A No."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Prosecution Witness Payam Akhavan. (Videotape played) "Q ... ethnically disparaging comments towards Muslims? A No, he did not. He was extremely polite."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Prosecution Witness Friis-Pedersen. (Videotape played) "Q ... conversations with Colonel Blaskic, did he ever threaten any harm towards ECMM, BritBat, or any other international organisation? A No. Q In fact, he cooperated with ECMM; wouldn't you agree with that? A It seemed so. Whenever we had a request, he tried to come forward to us and assist him."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Prosecution witness Alistair Duncan. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Is it fair to say that Colonel Blaskic never in any conversation with you spoke of Muslims with racial prejudice in his statement? A He was -- that's correct. Yes, that's correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Prosecution Witness Morsink. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q Were you ever told that Colonel Blaskic had made any inflammatory or derogatory marks on TV, radio, in speeches, or otherwise during your tour of duty? Did you ever receive such information? A Never."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Father Pervan, a witness of the Defence. (Videotape played) "A I never heard Mr. Blaskic say anything bad about any nationality or that he would give bad names to other -- members of other ethnic groups. I never heard him do anything of that kind."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Charles McLeod, a witness of the Prosecution. (Videotape played) "Mr. Hayman: Q At any point in the interview, did Colonel Blaskic express any ethnic animosity towards any ethnic group? A No. I think that he was saying to me that he felt that people ought to be able to live together."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Prosecutor alleged that Blaskic had ordered the crimes in Ahmici. What does Robert Stewart say, a Court witness? (Videotape played) "Judge Shahabuddeen: Was it your impression that he was upset to learn that grave crimes had been committed in Ahmici, or was he upset by the circumstance that you, a person whom he respected, was telling him this and demanding action? A I think he was upset by what had happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And again Bob Stewart. (Videotape played) "Mr. Kehoe: Q Now, you note in this particular document, that in fairness to Blaskic, I also told him that he seemed very shocked about it all. Do you see that line? A Yes. I do, and I wouldn't have written it unless I felt it, because, as I say, he's a decent man to me, and I was shocked, and he seemed shocked to too, because both of us had families, and I always felt that about Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what did Blaskic teach his soldiers? Witness DL. (Videotape played) "A '... those who are not collected and who might react to evil with a tenfold stronger evil without thinking about the innocent. My talk with you today and any other in the future will always be sharply in tune towards those who may be rash in that sense.' Q Please proceed. A 'We are not here in these uniforms and armed with rifles to attack the unarmed and the captured. I will never allow that. I will always ask you and my associates to respect this human rule.' Q Please proceed. A 'And for as long as I live, that is how I will try to influence my subordinates.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That was how the witness interpreted it, because he took note of Blaskic's speech to soldiers prior to sending them off to the front. Finally, Your Honours, when determining the criminal liability of Tihomir Blaskic, the Defence appeals to you to focus on him personally, to judge him, his acts, and his omissions, because Tihomir Blaskic is an honourable man and an honourable general. He was the first to surrender himself as soon as he heard that he had been indicted, and he came because he was ready to stand before you and to answer for his deeds or for his omissions, but not also for things that he personally is not responsible for and which were committed by others. Do not judge Blaskic as a symbol but as a man. Bosnia, and especially the war in Bosnia, and the crimes in Bosnia cannot be viewed in black and white clichés. They can be viewed rather like cowboy films, with good and bad guys, with the BH army being the good guy and the HVO the bad guy. It is not the HVO that committed the crime. The HVO is not a criminal organisation. There is no major criminal project. Crimes were committed by individuals with first and last names, and they must be called to account. The Prosecutor, in his closing arguments, asks you to react to an injustice committed against the Muslims in the Lasva Valley with another injustice. If the chain of injustices continues, then all hope for Bosnia-Herzegovina will be lost. Do not allow that to happen. Cut that chain of injustice now. Pass the right decision. Acquit General Blaskic. The Defence appeals that this Trial Chamber acquit General Blaskic. Your Honours, the Defence has hereby completed its closing arguments. We have done our best to assist you in your difficult task, indeed, and a responsible one, and from now on, we hand over the fate of our client into your hands, confident that justice will be served. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. Before closing the discussion, I have a minor technical problem to raise. Can we consider that the Defence and the Prosecution agree to delete certain motions that may have been left over? I think there are, Mr. Fourmy, two or three motions left that haven't been resolved. Mr. Fourmy?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a recent motion from the Defence under seal regarding the problem of translation. I don't know whether that still is an issue in view of what the parties have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you wish us to discuss -- of course, we're not going to discuss it today, the discussion is closed, but would you prefer that we respond to it in the final judgement? Do you wish to withdraw it? Do you insist upon it? Tell us quickly, because this is the occasion that we have to hear you. You will not be speaking again, in this case, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. President. This is a translation error, and there's a translation error that we drew your attention to in our motion. We would simply ask that you order that it be referred to the translation unit for any correction and that any corrected copy of the exhibit be entered into the record. That would resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection on the part of the Prosecution, I assume?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Since we weren't privy to the motion, Mr. President, it's hard to say we have no objection, so we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As this is being treated in public, let's make things quite clear. In that case, we can conclude that there are no motions pending and that the debate is closed. We agree, don't we, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think so, but the motion was not ex parte, so the Prosecutor should have the motion. It was filed and they should have it in their files. If they don't have a copy, perhaps the Registrar's office could assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'm going to pronounce the closure of the trial. It is true that we have come to the end of a long trip. I'm saying this for the public, which was rather numerous today and which was not always so, and this is only understandable because we have had 25 months of trial. I'm looking at some of the figures, like Mr. Nobilo. I know that we have 30.000 pages of transcript to read and that we had 223 days of hearings and we heard 558 witnesses, to complete a humane but a complex task, that is, to judge the defendant. Before really closing the debate, I wish to thank my colleagues, and I'm thinking in particular of Judge Riad who the public was able to see today on the screen but who has been indisposed and had to leave us. I also, of course, wish to thank the parties and the accused for agreeing to having him replaced, and he was not able to participate in this long journey with us throughout. I also wish to thank Almiro Rodrigues, who doesn't have 30.000 but 18.000 pages of transcript. I also thank the manner in which he immediately joined in the debate with such conviction. I wish to thank the attorneys too. You have demonstrated not only a great degree of competence and professional ability, but I also wish to thank you for devoting to these legal debates not only your legal competence, but also a very high courtesy, a high standard, which doesn't mean that there wasn't some lively exchanges between you, but that your relations were cordial, which is quite normal in a system of justice and especially international justice as this. Of course, I mustn't forget the interpreters and the court reporters, without whom we would not have been able to do much, and also the miracle of the technical booth. I heard myself speaking in absolute perfect English, which is a great accomplishment for me at the end of this lengthy debate. I also wish to underline that the accused also behaved in an exemplary manner, and this also contributed to the debates being clear and the easiness with which the Judges were able to rule. I cannot give you the date when the decision will be made. I can just tell you that the Judges of this Chamber, after a few days of holidays, will devote their full attention to this and provide General Blaskic with a ruling as soon as possible. Of course, Mr. Fourmy will inform you of the exact date. For all of those, who I hope are numerous here, who are looking forward to a few days of holiday, I wish to say that we will be thinking of them. We wish them all the best in the days that come, and I thank them all for their participation in this major trial that ends today. Thank you.
